content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

This is her anthem for what is about to unfold.

I’m stronger than I’ve been before.

We’re in a synagogue in the Upper West Side: Chava (Tommy Dorfman), a trans rabbi enters in a short dress, dancing and singing to Ariana Grande.

This is the part where I break free—

Jonah (Brandon Uranowitz), a contemporary rabbi who left Judaism and returned to the religion (apparantly common among rabbis), has built up this synagogue and agreed to meet Chava there to break the news to her father, Tati (Richard Schiff), that she is a woman.

Brandon Uranowitz (Jonah); Photo by Matthe Murphy

Richard Schiff enters in complete Hasidic Jewish men’s attire and sidelocks. Not only is Tati a prominent rabbi in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, but he descends from Baal Shen Tov, the very founder of Hasidic Judaism. He sees Chava as his first-born son. Tati is powerful, gentle, well-studied, and sees Jonah as a “heretic with a brain.” This entire cast is confident, sarcastic, and honest in one way or another.

Opening at a time of fierce urgency, Becoming Eve offers us poignant perspective of a female’s soul trapped in a Jewish boy’s body. It’s an intimate, engaging, and entertaining journey into the personal reincarnation of Transgender Rabbi Abby Stein, portrayed by Tommy Dorfman as “Chava.” Based on the memoir (by the same title) by Abby Chava Stein, Becoming Eve, is written for the stage by Emil Weinstein and directed by Tyne Rafaeli.

Initially set to run at The Connelly Theater, objections about the play’s subject of gender from the theater’s landlord forced Becoming Eve, produced by The New York Theatre Workshop, to find a new stage. Abrons Art Center holds a realistic, multi-functioning set, designed by Arnulfo Maldonado.

I am pleading with you.  Go see this production before it closes.

The casting could not be better. The characters feel natural. The ability for the actors to relate to the production’s topics of culture or gender adds a level of authenticity that made me feel comfortable to listen and learn. Chava and Tati’s intense, emotional moments of frustration and anger and shame were lovingly paternal–I needed to wipe tears from my eyes a few times…

Narratives of text and historical figures that developed Judaism lead digestible conversations between Chava and her father. I much appreciate that this performance did not once shine a negative light towards Judaism; rather, Chava is able to discover the pieces of text and narrative that connects her soul to Judaism even more.

Reb Nachman, the great grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, believed that Adam and Eve were created as one body, essentially split in half–and when Isaac, son of Abraham, was born, he was born with the soul of a female. Chava believes that reincarnation brings the soul of a female into a man.

But the part of this show that brought this show to the next level was the puppetry. Instead of using a child to depict young Chava, the puppets not only work theatrically but show the past iterations of Chava puppeteered to perform as a good Jewish son.

Just a flicker of the fluorescents take us from present to past and back again. Flawless. Even within seconds when sets are changed and Puppet Chava is replaced by Human Chava.

The puppetry works by two or three completely masked figures in black operating the puppets’ arms, legs, back, head, precisely holding young Chava up. As Chava grows, the puppet grows. Chava stands behind puppet and puppeteers, passionately delivering her own voice.

Justin Perkins, Tommy Dorfman and Judy Kuhn in flash back of Chava at age 2; Photo by Matthew Murphy

From two-year-old Chava, distraught about an upcoming haircut, to growing up in the shadow of Tati, to serving as a male Hasidic rabbi, we see Puppet Chava pray every night to be a girl, leave her community, and embrace the woman she is–all while she unearths and embraces her own identity in faith.

Justin Perkins, Tommy Dorfman and Richard Schiff, in a flashback of Chava at age 6; Photo by Matthew Murphy

As Chava digs deeper into her ancestor’s beliefs, she connects with Chesky (Rad Pereira), another future-rabbi navigating gender identity. In moments of vulnerability and truth, Human Chava replaces Puppet Chava. When Chesky and Chava kiss, it’s Human Chava’s lips. She’s no longer a puppet; she’s doing what she wants, not what her father wants his son to do. These moments are the most beautiful.

Chava marries Fraidy (Tedra Millan); their time together is sincere and holds gravity. Fraidy’s willing to embrace Chava if Chava is willing to be herself here, in their home.

“What if I change so much you aren’t allowed to love me?”

Tommy Dorfman, Tedra Millan, Emma Perkins and Justin Perkins, in flashback of Chava and Fraidy’s wedding night; Photo by Matthew Murphy

Chava’s Jewish identity simultaneously pulls her back and propels her forward. We see how culture, beliefs, and self can altogether merge and collide head on. We watch Chava break down on a Bronx dance floor, Jewish melodies still playing in the background.

Sometimes, we just need to digest the text, outside of traditional instruction, on our journey to  identifying ourselves.

 

“The easy path is not often the right path to take. It is the very obstacles that make life difficult that also make us who we are.”

— The Baal Shem Tov.

 

Based on the memoir, Becoming Eve, by Abby Chava Stein.

Written by Emil Weinstein; Directed by Tyne Rafaeli.

CAST: Tommy Dorfman (Chava), Judy Kuhn (Mami), Tedra Millan (Fraidy), Rad Pereira (Chesky), Justin Otaki Perkins (Puppeteer), Richard Schiff (Tati), Brandon Uranowitz (Jonah), Emma Wiseman (Puppeteer).

CREATIVE TEAM: Arnulfo Maldonado (Scenic Design), Enver Chakartash (Costume Design), Ben Stanton (Lighting Design), Uptown Works (Sound Design), Amanda Villalobos (Puppetry Design & Direction).

Becoming Eve is playing at Abrons Arts Center in Manhattan’s Lower East Side, 466 Grand St., New York, NY, through April 27, 2025. Run time is an hour and 45 minutes with no intermission.

content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

In David Mamet’s Glengarry Glen Ross, everybody wants to talk. “Listen to me.” “You gotta hear this.” “Let me tell you something.” In this revival on Broadway, directed by Patrick Marber and starring Bob Odenkirk, Kieran Culkin, and Bill Burr, we’re here to listen.

In this play, everyone’s desperate to sell. What they’re selling is worthless land to people who can’t afford it. What they’re chasing is something simple yet slippery: money. The story is told with precision and clarity. The direction is lean, the acting exact, and the result is excellent—and, surprisingly, poignant.

How do you sell? You gotta have the “premium leads.” The first act is a series of two-handers in a Chinese restaurant. A spotlight marks each scene, keeping the focus squarely on the words and performance. Shelley Levene (Bob Odenkirk) used to have his touch; it’s gone now. He’s begging for a second chance, pleading with office manager Williamson (Donald Webber Jr.) for leads. Odenkirk’s Levene is, right off the bat, a catastrophe of neediness. A man for whom selling has become not merely livelihood but existential affirmation. Odenkirk inhabits this desperation so completely, so fully, it grabs you immediately.

We move to Moss (Bill Burr) and Aaronow (Michael McKean). Moss suggests they rob the office, steal the leads, and sell them. Burr’s clarity with the text occasionally falters, and he pushes a little too hard, but the music of the exchange remains intact, with McKean providing a hesitant counterpoint.

Completing the first act’s triptych of scenes is Richard Roma (Kieran Culkin) seducing potential buyer Lingk (John Pirruccello) with philosophical musings that would leave Kant flummoxed: “You fuck little girls, so be it. There’s an absolute morality? May be. And then what?” Culkin is perhaps a bit too subdued in this now-famous monologue, but he wakes up in the second act when the stakes heighten.

The first act builds. The second explodes. We’re in the office, the morning after a break-in. All the salesmen are there, moving in and out, circling each other, while Detective Baylen (Howard W. Overshown) attempts, and mostly fails, to take control.

While the ensemble is strong across the board, Odenkirk’s Shelley Levene is impossible to look away from. It’s astonishing that this is his Broadway debut. When he bursts into the second act, transformed by an $82,000 sale, Odenkirk performs a kind of incandescent aria. Then he stages his mini show-within-a-show to Roma, reenacting how he closed the deal—he’s back in business. This moment evokes the Player’s speech in Hamlet, and you want to say, as the young prince does, “Say on; come to Hecuba.” Come to Hecuba, Bob. Only Mamet’s Hecuba is a Florida condo and a pen to seal the deal.

Soon after, Lingk—whom Roma convinced to buy—arrives at the office. He’s nervous and fidgety, carrying a mission from his wife: cancel the sale. Here, Culkin locks in, revealing just how much he and his cronies dupe these poor would-be owners. It’s heartbreaking when Lingk quietly confesses, “I can’t negotiate. I don’t have the power.” He’s not just asking to back out, he’s also apologizing; Roma has created a scenario where ethics are turned upside down.

Then comes the devastating blow that, with Odenkirk’s performance, lifts it all to tragic heights. Levene’s deal is revealed to be worthless. The elderly couple he sold to is lonely and never had the money. They just liked the company. Odenkirk makes this crushing failure visceral: the initial desperation, the fleeting joy, the catastrophic fall—a performance of extraordinary architecture and energy that lifts the role to classic stature.

This isn’t a Greek tragedy of kings brought down by fate. It’s a tragedy of salesmen, undone by money. There’s no death here. Just lost hope, unearned rewards, and at the end of the day, no Cadillac.

There’s real relief in Marber’s crystalline approach: the text, the acting, and the timeless struggle for worth. The Palace Theatre was packed the day I attended, with lines for merchandise. What do you expect? Stars want to act in it. Audiences want to hear it. Not an empty seat in the house.

GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS by David Mamet; Directed by Patrick Marber.

With: Bob Odenkirk, Donald Webber Jr., Bill Burr, Michael McKean, Kieran Culkin, John Pirruccello, Howard W. Overshown

Sets and Costume Design by John Pask. Lighting Design by Jen Schriever.

Now playing through June 28 at Palace Theatre, 160 W 47th St. Tickets available here.

Run time: 105 minutes, including a 15-minute intermission.

title.rendered: Tapping into the Twenties: The ASO and Forgotten Marvels at David Geffen Hall

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

This past Sunday afternoon, the newly transformed David Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center pulsed with the energy of the Roaring Twenties. But this was no costume party of musical nostalgia. The American Symphony Orchestra, under the inspired baton of Leon Botstein, offered something far more nourishing: a sweeping, intelligent, and emotionally resonant exploration of rarely performed masterworks in a program aptly titled Tapping into the Twenties.

Here’s a sample of the concert:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by American Symphony Orchestra (@americansymphony)

This concert was more than a performance—it was a reclamation. It was a sonic time capsule cracked open to reveal truths about modernity, identity, and innovation. The music unfurled like a collection of innovative and creative hallmarks of the ASO’s psyche—each work from a different angle in the fractured mirror of the interwar period.

Leon Botstein’s Vision: The Genius of the Unfamiliar

Long before the downbeat, the audience was treated to conductor Leon Botstein’s signature Conductor’s Notes Q&A session at 2 p.m. With his characteristic blend of scholarly rigor and avuncular wit, Botstein transformed a pre-concert chat into an essential act of musical excavation. He painted the concert’s historical canvas vividly—linking the chaos and creativity of the 1920s to the expressive urgency heard in the evening’s works.

His passion for resurrecting unjustly forgotten music is not merely a mission; it’s a moral imperative. Through Botstein’s lens, the 1920s emerge not as a single genre or style but as a collision of divergent energies—futurism, jazz, machine-age industrialism, mysticism, and cultural hybridism.

A concert of enigmatic works performed with alacrity emerged, threading between formal disruption and lyrical soul.

Leon Botstein. Photo by Matt Dine

John Alden Carpenter’s Skyscrapers: The Urban Ballet in Full Swing

Opening the concert, Skyscrapers: A Ballet of Modern American Life by John Alden Carpenter proved a stunning curtain-raiser. Premiered in 1926, this music is part Copland, part Chaplin—yet unmistakably Carpenter, the industrialist, laying out America’s new mythos in steel, speed, and syncopation.

Unfinished portrait of John Alden Carpenter (1921). Public Domain via Wikipedia Commons

The American Symphony Orchestra gave this work the technicolor treatment it demands. The percussion was crisp and driving, echoing the mechanized rhythms of a newly electrified nation. Strings shimmered with restraint, then soared with Broadway gusto. Carpenter’s bifurcated portrait of Work and Play came alive in this performance—with factory clangor morphing seamlessly into ragtime playfulness.

Glistening soundscapes of programmatic landscapes emerged—urban life rendered in orchestral brushstrokes. Concertmaster Cyrus Beroukhim imbued the violin solos with elegance and wit, anchoring the shifting moods with remarkable poise.

Schulhoff’s Jazz Concerto and Orion Weiss’s Dazzling Performance

Enter Erwin Schulhoff, the Czech-born avant-gardist who danced with Dadaism, jazz, and tragedy. His Concerto for Piano and Small Orchestra, Op. 43 is a brash, soulful, and structurally audacious work that thumbs its nose at bourgeois tradition while inviting jazz into the concert hall with revolutionary fervor.

Composer Ervín Schulhoff (1894–1942) and dancer Milča Mayerová (1901-1977), ca 1931. Anonymous/Unknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Pianist Orion Weiss was incandescent. From the concerto’s gauzy opening to the syncopated, biting Allegro alla Jazz, he summoned the ghost of George Antheil with the lyricism of Debussy and the rhythmic swagger of Fats Waller—Weiss’s flawless pianistic technique allowed for no barriers between the score and its expressive potential.

Orion Weiss, Piano. Photo by Lisa Marie Mazzucco.

The ASO’s chamber-sized forces responded with timbral clarity and rhythmic tension. Weiss’s cadenza was a spiritual séance, channeling the melancholy of a continent on the brink. It wasn’t just entertainment—it was history made audible.

Weiss offered Schulhoff’s 1929 Sentimental Melody as a radiant encore, a brief yet poignant slice of irony and tenderness that offered a final wink from a decade caught between dreams and disillusionment.

Arcana: The Thunder of Edgard Varèse

Edgard Varèse once claimed, “Music is organized sound.” His 1927 behemoth Arcana takes that principle to the edge of apocalypse.

From the opening percussion blasts to the massive climactic dissonances, the American Symphony Orchestra sculpted Varèse’s “sound masses” like sonic architecture. The anger and dissonance of Varèse’s work rose from the pit like some Promethean creature—half-machine, half-prophet.

The expanded percussion section was mesmerizing for its thunder and its sensitivity to dynamic range. Botstein masterfully balanced the tumult. The textures never devolved into noise but danced between chaos and coherence on the razor’s edge.

Where Schoenberg intellectualized dissonance through serialism, Varèse weaponized it—blurring the line between rhythm and roar.

Portrait of Edgar Varèse (1924) by John Sloan. Public Domain via Wikimedia Commons

William Grant Still’s Afro-American Symphony: A Heartfelt Benediction

To conclude the afternoon, Botstein turned to William Grant Still—the first African American composer to have a symphony performed by a major orchestra. His Afro-American Symphony remains a singular achievement: an elegant fusion of classical symphonic form and African American idioms.

The orchestra’s rendering was radiant and deeply affectionate. The first movement’s blues theme was warm and lyrical, while the second embraced spirituals with hushed reverence. The third burst with ragtime energy, and the finale—dignified and hymn-like—brought tears to eyes and cheers to lips.

It was the sound of a people, a history, and a hope—music of remembrance and resistance.

A Space Reborn: David Geffen Hall’s Acoustic Renaissance

The newly renovated David Geffen Hall is no mere facelift but an acoustic rebirth. The warmth and detail of the hall’s sonic profile now rival Europe’s best. Every pizzicato, every timpani roll emerged crystalline and immediate.

Its design now invites not only sound but spirit. From the comfortable seating to the golden, undulating walls, the venue wraps you in its arms. It is the perfect setting for a program as kaleidoscopic and historically vital as Tapping into the Twenties.

Program Notes and Thematic Programming: A Masterclass in Musicology

Special praise belongs to the program note authors, Colin Roust and Sebastian Danila, who provided essential context with clarity and insight. Their writing bridged the academic and the accessible, enhancing the audience’s journey.

This thoughtful contextualization is part of the American Symphony Orchestra’s DNA. Their programs are never mere concerts. They are seminars, narratives, and conversations with history.

Why the Twenties Still Matter: The Legacy of Innovation

Tapping into the Twenties revealed—through Carpenter’s urban vitality, Schulhoff’s radical hybridity, Varèse’s structural revolution, and Still’s cultural synthesis—that the 1920s were not only roaring. They were reckoning.

As the 19th century’s romanticism yielded to serialist codes and mechanized futures, some composers found a third path: expressive freedom fused with cultural consciousness. Schulhoff and Carpenter sidestepped Schoenberg’s tone rows with jazz and groove. Varèse exploded musical structures altogether. Still dignified the American vernacular.

Much like Kandinsky’s forays into abstraction, these composers sought spiritual meaning in color and form. They chased modern truths through sound—fragmented, ecstatic, restless, but always human.

American Symphony Orchestra. Courtesy americansymphony.org

A Final Note of Thanks

This concert was a triumph of vision, musicianship, and soul. The American Symphony Orchestra continues to illuminate the overlooked corners of musical history with rare conviction. Leon Botstein remains a national treasure. And David Geffen Hall has never sounded better.

We left the hall with hearts stirred, minds awakened, and more profound gratitude for the power of rediscovery.

Tapping into the Twenties: The ASO and Forgotten Marvels at David Geffen Hall

American Symphony Orchestra

1330 Avenue of the Americas
Suite 23A, New York, NY 10019
212.868.9276
For information and tickets, email info@americansymphony.org, or click HERE.

Readers may also enjoy Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra’s Immersive Journey and American Classical Orchestra: J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion.

The American Symphony Orchestra, under the inspired baton of Leon Botstein, offered something far more nourishing: a sweeping, intelligent, and emotionally resonant exploration of rarely performed masterworks in a program aptly titled Tapping into the Twenties.

title.rendered: Gabrielle Stravelli at Birdland Jazz Club NYC

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

Tonight was a Night to Remember—Gabrielle Stravelli’s Spellbinding Set at Birdland Jazz Club. Jazz vocalist Gabrielle Stravelli has always carried the torch of the American Songbook with elegance and an unmistakable voice that sparkles with charm, authenticity, and life. At her recent performance at Birdland Jazz Club, Stravelli did far more than entertain—she enraptured. With a keen sense of drama, humor, and a voice that could melt or invigorate, she delivered a vocal jazz performance that reminded us why live music remains irreplaceable.

Gabrielle Stravelli. Courtesy gabriellestravelli.com

From the moment Gabrielle Stravelli walked on stage, the sold-out audience at the iconic venue was already hers. Adorned in timeless flair, her luminous presence instantly set the tone for a memorable evening. But as Leonard Feather might say, a singer is only as good as the band behind her—and this band was extraordinary.

L-R: Pianist Willerm Delisfort, Gabrielle Stravelli, Bassist Pat O’Leary, and Trumpeter Ian Cleaver. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The Quintessential Jazz Combo Supporting Gabrielle Stravelli’s Artistic Brilliance

Bassist Pat O’Leary

On bass, the ever-steady and inventive Pat O’Leary brought the finesse that only musical brilliance and decades of experience can provide. O’Leary, a former Clark Terry, and James Moody collaborator arranged many of the evening’s selections. His bass lines in “Day In, Day Out” propelled the groove while offering melodic counterpoints to the vocals.

Perhaps most striking was his work on “Kiss and Run,” when she evoked a heartfelt, dark, and rich sonic narrative with narrative tension. With Gabrielle Stravelli’s haunting vocals atop it, the number felt like a noir film unfolding in real-time.

Pianist Willerm Delisfort

Pianist Willerm Delisfort’s nimble fingers seemed to anticipate Stravelli’s phrasing before it was sung. Delisfort has performed with luminaries such as Donald Harrison and Marcus Printup. His playing is characterized by elegance, modern sensitivity, and gospel-inflected grooves. At Birdland, he glided from impressionistic chords, extended solos, and trading with O’Leary to daring runs, matching Gabrielle Stravelli’s improvisational spirit note for note.

On Ellington’s “Warm Valley,” Delisfort’s intro alone transported us into a smoky 1940s Harlem nightclub. His harmonies dripped with romantic nuance, painting the perfect canvas for Stravelli’s custom-penned lyrics.

L-R: Bassist Pat O’Leary Courtesy SoapBox Gallery. Photo by Lynn Redmile. Willerm Delisfort, Pianist. Courtesy @wdelisfort on Instagram. Trumpeter Ian Cleaver. Courtesy @ianraycleaver on Instagram

Trumpeter Ian Cleaver

Then there was guest artist Ian Cleaver, the young Dutch trumpeter whose mature tone and lyrical sense belie his age. Known for his work with the Jazz Orchestra of the Concertgebouw, Cleaver’s approach is conversational, understated, and drenched in soul.

On Roye Alfred’s “Kiss and Run,” Cleaver’s subtle, tasty offerings danced around Gabrielle Stravelli’s luminous vocal lines that evoked the themes of fleeting romance. Stravelli portrayed the tensions between seduction and sadness, masking it with a swing feel that contrasted the emotional undercurrent. Cleaver’s sensitivity contributed to one of the night’s most magical moments.

Gabrielle Stravelli: Keeper of the Songbook and Inventor of New Moods

The set list was a tour through the American Songbook and beyond, yet Gabrielle Stravelli reshaped every tune to reflect her distinct artistic fingerprint. From Marvin Fisher’s wistful “It Could Happen to You” to Carolyn Leigh’s buoyant defiance of “I’ve Got Your Number,” she infused each lyric with fresh emotional clarity.

Throughout the evening, her interpretive power made every listener feel as if the song had been written for them—and for this moment.

The vocal acrobatics in “Born to Be Blue” showcased her impeccable control and jazz phrasing. Meanwhile, her comedic timing in “Down With Love” lit up the room, bridging heartbreak and hilarity in the space of a few bars.

Here’s a segment from Stravelli’s performance at Birdland earlier this month:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Gabrielle Stravelli (@gabriellestravelli)

The Rhythmic Pulse: Drive and Cultural Resonance

No moment encapsulated the evening’s rhythmic drive and emotional intensity like “Someday Sweetheart.” Originally a Benny Goodman standard, Stravelli’s rendition revitalized it “a la Ella,” giving it new pop culture relevance and a deep groove. This song has crossed the line between swing-era elegance and modern-day heartache, and under Gabrielle Stravelli’s artistic direction, it felt like a cathartic release.

Similarly, “Moon River” has long been a cultural icon, inseparably tied to Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Yet in Stravelli’s interpretation, it became a conversation—between past and present, nostalgia and discovery. It was sublime, passionate, and profoundly moving.

The Enduring Appeal of Gabrielle Stravelli

Gabrielle Stravelli is not just a performer but an artist, storyteller, and guardian of the jazz tradition. Over the years, she has shared stages with Wynton Marsalis, headlined international festivals, and released critically acclaimed albums, including Dream Ago and the stirring new release Beautiful Moons Ago.

Her accolades include the 2019 Bistro Award for Outstanding Recording and the 2017 MAC Award for Best Vocal Jazz Performance. But beyond the trophies and glowing reviews, her authenticity endears her to fans. Gabrielle Stravelli sings to connect, uplift, and tell the truth—sometimes with tears, other times with laughter.

Gabrielle Stravelli. Courtesy SoapBox Gallery. Photo by Lynn Redmile

Humor and Humanity On Stage

There was a moment during the set when Stravelli, reflecting on love gone wrong, quipped, “Yes, those are my people,” to an audience member who had sighed in recognition. It was more than comic relief—a bridge between the artist and the audience. She is as much at home among broken hearts as she is among lovers and jazz connoisseurs.

Her rapport with her bandmates—whether trading solos, echoing melodies, or playfully teasing a phrase—is electrifying. Their chemistry is so seamless that it seems almost telepathic.

Birdland Jazz Club: A Home for Greatness

No review of this performance would be complete without praising Birdland Jazz Club. The acoustics are pristine, the sightlines ideal, and the intimate ambiance unmatched. This legendary venue continues to nurture jazz excellence in New York, and Gabrielle Stravelli’s performance reminded us why it’s one of the world’s most respected jazz stages.

The Songs, the Stories, and the Soul of Gabrielle Stravelli

Gabrielle Stravelli doesn’t just sing a song—she lives it, reinvents it, and delivers it with a universal and profoundly personal warmth. Whether it’s a heartbreak ballad, a whimsical swing, or a cinematic lullaby, she lends clarity, purpose, and honesty.

Throughout the evening, songs stood out for their lyrical depth, emotional impact, and rhythmic excitement. Each was a masterclass in jazz storytelling. As Leonard Feather might have written, “It’s not just what she sings—it’s how she means it.” She truly does!

Beautiful Moons Ago album on Spotify

One Night, Infinite Reverberations

By the night’s end, the audience rose not out of obligation but gratitude for having experienced something real, poignant, and unrepeatable. Gabrielle Stravelli gave them jazz with a heartbeat, and they responded in kind—with applause, cheers, and tearful eyes.

Now is the time to discover Gabrielle Stravelli—hear her live, buy her recordings, and fall in love with jazz again. For her Tour Dates, click Here .

Readers may also enjoy Melvis Santa’s Jazz Orishas Magic and the Kenny Barron Trio at Smoke Jazz Club.

title.rendered: SurRound II: Divine Sonic Tapestry at St. John the Divine

content.rendered:
In the vast, resonant expanse of the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, Musica Sacra, under the inspired direction of Kent Tritle, delivered a SurRound II concert of such ethereal beauty that time itself seemed suspended. The packed audience sat transfixed, many with eyes closed, as waves of a cappella voices washed over them from different points in the magnificent space. This innovative surround sound concept transformed the impressive cathedral into an immersive sonic environment that elevated the sacred texts to extraordinary heights.

Maestro Kent Tritle. Photo by Jennifer Taylor

Allegri’s “Miserere”: Transcendent Sonic Prayers

The concert began with Gregorio Allegri’s legendary “Miserere,” a work of such jealously guarded beauty that the Vatican once forbade its transcription. Nevertheless, as musical lore recounts, a young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart famously committed the entire piece to memory after a single hearing at the Sistine Chapel. Rachel Doehring Jackson’s soprano soared effortlessly to the work’s famous high C, her crystalline tone floating above the perfectly balanced choir with angelic purity.

The “Miserere,” a penitential setting of Psalm 51, has been a centerpiece of Holy Week services for centuries. Its alternating choirs created a spatial dialogue that perfectly suited the surround sound concept. Jackson’s soprano rode above the ensemble with flawless intonation, her expressive phrasing illuminating the text’s pleas for mercy and spiritual cleansing. The choir’s supporting voices created a velvet cushion of sound. Their precision in dynamics and articulation revealed musical sophistication and spiritual depth.

L-R: Soprano Rachel Doehring Jackson (Photo by Jessica Osber Photography), and Soprano Kathryn McCreary. (Courtesy kathrynmccreary.com)

 

Stellar Soloists Shine Throughout SurRound II

Each soloist brought distinctive artistry to the SurRound II program. Following the Gregorian chant “Da Pacem, Domine,” Kathryn McCreary’s soprano and Oliver Holt’s warm, resonant baritone brought profound emotion to Adolphus Hailstork’s “Motherless Child.” Their voices complemented each other perfectly, and the spiritual lament was rendered with authentic feeling and technical excellence.

Helen Karloski’s mezzo-soprano proved particularly moving in Tavener’s “Lament of the Mother of God.” Her rich, burnished tone conveyed Mary’s aching grief at the crucifixion with remarkable emotional intensity. Moreover, her flawless control of the work’s demanding extended lines created a hypnotic effect that held the audience spellbound.

Mezzo Soprano Helen Karloski (Courtesy helenkarloski.com) and Baritone Oliver Holt (Courtesy Oliver Holt)

Later in the program, Katherine Wessinger’s soprano and Paul D’Arcy’s tenor illuminated Holst’s “Nunc Dimittis.” Their voices emerged from and blended into the choir seamlessly, exemplifying the ensemble’s extraordinary attention to balance and blend.

Tenor Paul Darcy (Courtesy @pauldarcy on Instagram, and Soprano Katherine Wessinger (Courtesy katherinewessinger.com

Medieval Masterworks: SurRound II’s Journey Through Time

Perhaps the evening’s most fascinating historical offering was Perotin’s “Sederunt,” a revolutionary work from the 12th century. The voices of Musica Sacra created an extraordinary drone effect, supporting the soloist with perfect pitch matching that transported listeners to the medieval Notre Dame Cathedral. This revolutionary four-voice organum, with its intricate triplet figures, received a performance of remarkable historical accuracy and expressive power.

The SurRound II program masterfully interwove ancient and modern works. Gregorian chants served as palate-cleansing interludes between more complex compositions. “Pange lingua gloriosi” led seamlessly into Sarah MacDonald’s contemporary “Crux Fidelis,” a striking juxtaposition that illustrated how modern composers continue to find inspiration in ancient sacred texts.

The Cathedral: Perfect Vessel for SurRound II’s Sonic Explorations

The Cathedral of St. John the Divine’s 601-foot length and soaring 124-foot ceiling provided the ideal acoustic environment for this ambitious SurRound II presentation. Though still technically unfinished, the world’s largest Gothic cathedral offers a reverberant acoustic that enhances rather than muddles choral sound. Consequently, even the most complex polyphonic textures remained distinct while gaining a numinous glow from the space.

As choir members moved to different positions throughout the cathedral during the SurRound II performance, listeners experienced an actual surround-sound effect that electronically amplified performances can never replicate. The singers occasionally positioned themselves among the audience, creating an extraordinary sense of inclusion in the sonic experience. This innovative approach transformed the concert from a mere performance to a communal ritual.

Pérotin in the 13th century. Public Domain

O Nata Lux: Immersed in Radiance

One of the evening’s most intimate and powerful moments came during Eric Whitacre’s “O nata lux.” The choir positioned themselves directly among the audience, surrounding listeners with crystalline harmonies from all directions. This configuration created an extraordinary sense of being enveloped in sonic light, perfectly complementing the text’s invocation of divine radiance. Several audience members visibly wept during this profoundly moving performance.

The SurRound II program skillfully traced a journey from penitence to illumination, mirroring the Lenten season’s progression toward Easter’s promise of renewal. William L. Dawson’s spiritual “Soon ah will be done” and Joanna Forbes L’Estrange’s “Give Us Grace” provided contrasting expressions of spiritual yearning, both performed with impeccable attention to rhythmic vitality and textual clarity.

SurRound II: Sonic Time Travel Through Sacred Music

The diverse SurRound II program created what can be described as musical time travel, spanning nearly a millennium of sacred composition. From Perotin’s 12th-century innovations to contemporary works by Whitacre and MacDonald, the concert demonstrated the evolution and continuity of sacred choral traditions. Furthermore, including spirituals alongside European sacred music emphasized the universal human impulse to express spiritual longing through song.

Many listeners appeared overcome by the music’s emotional power, transported beyond everyday concerns into contemplative states. This transcendent effect—difficult to achieve in our distraction-filled world—testifies to both the repertoire’s inherent power and the exceptional artistry of the performers. The SurRound II concept amplified this effect by literally surrounding the audience with sound from multiple directions, creating an immersive experience impossible to replicate through recordings.

Cathedral of St. John the Divine, New York, N. Y (NYPL b12647398-66417). Detroit Publishing Company, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Kent Tritle: Masterful Architect of Sound and Space

Kent Tritle’s masterful direction revealed his exceptional understanding of musical architecture and acoustic space. His expressive conducting elicited performances of remarkable precision and emotional depth. Moreover, his innovative use of the cathedral’s geography in this SurRound II presentation demonstrated why he remains one of America’s most respected choral conductors.

Tritle’s imaginative programming created a cohesive journey through disparate musical eras and styles. Each work received its distinct character while contributing to the overall spiritual and musical narrative. His deep knowledge of sacred music traditions informed every performance aspect, from tempi to text emphasis to spatial positioning.

The choir responded to his nuanced direction with extraordinary sensitivity and technical expertise. Their unified articulation, dynamics, and phrasing approach revealed intensive preparation and in-the-moment responsiveness. Even in the cathedral’s challenging acoustic, entrances remained crisp, consonants clear, and harmonies perfectly tuned.

A Transcendent SurRound II Experience

As the final notes of “O nata lux” faded into the cathedral’s vaulted heights, a profound silence held the audience motionless before erupting into heartfelt applause. Musica Sacra’s SurRound II had achieved that rarest of musical experiences—a performance that transcends technical excellence to become spiritual communication.

In our fragmented modern world, such moments of unified attention and shared emotion have become increasingly precious. This extraordinary surround sound concert demonstrated why live choral music in sacred spaces continues to move human hearts across centuries and cultures. As audience members reluctantly departed the cathedral after a well-earned encore, many lingered, clearly hoping to extend the evening’s enchantment just a little longer.

For those fortunate enough to experience this remarkable SurRound II presentation, the memory will remain a touchstone of musical and spiritual transcendence—a reminder of music’s power to illuminate our shared humanity and connect us to something beyond ourselves.

SurRound II: Divine Sonic Tapestry at St. John the Divine

Mark Hanke, Executive Director
Kent Tritle, Music Director
Michael Sheetz, Assistant Music Director

title.rendered: In the Shadow of Memory: “Remembrance” at Theater for the New City

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

Remembrance is a heart-rending portrait of caregiving and loss, with Black Box brilliance that delivers intimate theater of uncommon power.

Harrowing and Strangely Affirming

A particular alchemy exists within the confines of a black box theater, where the absence of spectacle forces an audience into direct communion with raw human truth. At Theater for the New City, Patricia Goodson’s “Remembrance” harnesses this intimate power to devastating effect. The production eschews theatrical artifice in favor of something far more precious: authentic emotional resonance. Indeed, this stark examination of caregiving amidst the cruel progression of Alzheimer’s disease offers audiences an experience that is at once harrowing and strangely affirming.

The immediacy of the black box setting proves ideal for “Remembrance,” allowing audience members to witness every flicker of emotion across the performers’ faces. Within this confined space, the claustrophobic reality of long-term caregiving becomes palpable—we are not merely spectators but unwitting participants in this family’s unraveling. Furthermore, the minimal staging, with its three distinct playing areas (doctors’ offices, patient’s room, and family living room), underscores the fragmented consciousness at the heart of this narrative.

L-R: Bryn Eva O’Connor, Beth Griffith, Kkuumba Siegell in a scene from Remembrance at the Theater for the New City. Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

Beth Griffith’s Moma: A Heartbreaking Journey Through Time and Memory

In the demanding role of Moma, Beth Griffith delivers a performance of exceptional nuance and devastating authenticity. Her portrayal of a woman disappearing into the fog of Alzheimer’s avoids the maudlin sentimentality that often plagues depictions of dementia. Instead, she offers something far more profound: a portrait of diminishment that nevertheless contains glimpses of the vibrant woman who once was.

Particularly affecting are the moments when Griffith transports us back to her character’s childhood in war-torn Germany. As she recounts memories of oppression, death, and destruction in her native tongue, Griffith achieves a remarkable duality—embodying both the confused elderly woman of the present and the frightened child of the past. Moreover, her unexpected bursts of German folk songs provide bittersweet moments of clarity amidst the mental disintegration, reminding us how music often survives in memory long after other faculties have faded.

Beth Griffith in a scene from Remembrance at the Theater for the New City. Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

The Cruel Music of Decline: Mozart’s Adagio as Metaphor

Perhaps the production’s most poignant theatrical conceit occurs when Moma, seemingly lucid for a fleeting moment, begins to dance to the exquisite Adagio from Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 21. Griffith moves with a grace that momentarily belies her character’s condition, creating a heartbreaking illusion of wellness. However, as the beautiful Mozartian phrases gradually distort into cacophony, her movements become correspondingly erratic and confused. This masterful sequence is the perfect metaphor for Alzheimer’s inexorable progression—beauty collapsing into dissonance, order into chaos.

Director Joan Kane demonstrates remarkable sensitivity in this scene, allowing it to unfold without unnecessary embellishment. Her restrained approach throughout “Remembrance” reflects a deep understanding that the subject requires no theatrical amplification to achieve its emotional impact. Indeed, Kane’s direction consistently prioritizes emotional truth over melodramatic effect, allowing the audience genuine access to the complicated feelings that accompany witnessing a loved one’s mental deterioration.

The Dual Amys: Presenting the Divided Self of Caregiving

The decision to cast two actresses (Zane Julia and Bryn Eva O’Connor) as Amy—Moma’s daughter during different phases of her caregiving journey—proves remarkably effective. This theatrical device eloquently conveys the bifurcation of self that many caregivers experience: the public persona maintaining composure versus the private self-drowning in grief and exhaustion. Julia and O’Connor navigate this challenging dynamic with impressive synchronicity, creating a seamless portrait of a woman gradually unraveling under the strain of witnessing her mother’s deterioration.

David Odukoya in a scene from Remembrance at the Theater for the New City, Zane Julia. Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

The production benefits immensely from the contributions of David Odukoya as Doctor Blake and Kkuumba Siegell as Nadine, the professional caregiver whose spirituality and kindness counter Amy’s despair. Siegell, in particular, brings warmth and wisdom to her role, embodying the support systems that can emerge amid seemingly hopeless situations.

Doctor Blake: The Witness and Vessel for Caregiver’s Trauma

David Odukoya’s Doctor Blake transcends a mere narrative device, providing the essential framework through which Amy’s fragmented caregiving experiences coalesce into understanding. Odukoya navigates a delicate balance—maintaining professional distance while establishing a genuine connection—with remarkable subtlety, skillfully avoiding clinical detachment and excessive sentimentality.

Kkuumba Siegell, Bryn Eva O’Connor in a scene from Remembrance at the Theater for the New City. Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

As the audience’s surrogate, Doctor Blake poses the questions we might ask, comprehending clinical realities without becoming insensitive to suffering. In one powerful scene, when Amy describes her mother’s failure to recognize her, Odukoya’s response—merely a slight postural shift and momentary eye closure—communicates profound empathy. Such restraint creates space for Amy’s revelations to resonate authentically.

The therapy sessions brilliantly illuminate secondary trauma, with Doctor Blake guiding Amy to recognize her PTSD symptoms from years of witnessing her mother’s decline. Odukoya skillfully portrays this therapeutic journey from Amy’s initial resistance to her gradual acknowledgment of how her mother’s illness has reshaped her identity.

Most importantly, Doctor Blake represents essential support systems for caregivers, embodying society’s potential for genuine recognition of caregiving’s psychological toll rather than offering empty platitudes. His character ultimately catalyzes Amy’s psychological integration—her realization that profound loss and meaningful connection can coexist.

A Theater of Witness: The Audience Experience of “Remembrance”

Throughout the performance, one could observe audience members transfixed by the unfolding drama, many visibly moved by this unflinching portrayal of a daughter and mother navigating the cruelest of diseases. “Remembrance” achieves that rare theatrical alchemy that transforms individual suffering into collective catharsis. Inviting spectators to witness this intimate portrait of decline creates a space for communal recognition of our shared vulnerability.

The play’s moments of profound sadness are occasionally leavened by unexpected humor and tenderness, preventing “Remembrance” from becoming an exercise in unrelenting grimness. As Moma shares her butterfly metaphor—”When you see butterflies, you see Angel wings, and it means God is looking after you”—the production acknowledges how meaning and beauty can persist even in devastating loss.

L-R: Beth Griffith, Bryn Eva O’Connor in a scene from Remembrance at the Theater for the New City. Photo by Jonathan Slaff.

Reflecting Our Aging Society: The Timeliness of “Remembrance”

In an era when millions of aging Baby Boomers face potential cognitive decline, “Remembrance” arrives as a necessary examination of the often-overlooked caregiving crisis that accompanies Alzheimer’s disease. While numerous films and plays have explored dementia from the patient’s perspective, Goodson’s focus on the caregiver’s experience—captured in the devastating line “my mother has Alzheimers, so, therefore, do I”—addresses a critical gap in our cultural conversation about aging and illness.

Patricia Goodson’s script, born from her twelve-year journey with her own mother’s Alzheimer’s, exhibits the kind of hard-earned authenticity that cannot be simulated. Having previously explored similar themes through the more whimsical lens of her debut play “Aging is Not a Fairy Tale,” Goodson now confronts the subject with unflinching directness. Nevertheless, she infuses “Remembrance” with profound hope amidst the sorrow, reminding us that “our caring is our control and our bonds of love… are our weapons of defense.”

Theater for the New City: A Vital Space for Authentic Voices

Once again, Theater for the New City demonstrates its vital role in nurturing emerging playwrights and presenting works that confront uncomfortable truths with honesty and compassion. Under the stewardship of Executive Artistic Director Crystal Field, the theater’s Emerging Playwrights Program continues to cultivate diverse voices like Goodson’s, allowing deeply personal narratives to find their theatrical expression.

“Remembrance” exemplifies the kind of brave, timely, and socially relevant work that has been the hallmark of Theater for the New City for decades. By providing a platform for stories that mainstream theaters might consider too uncomfortable or commercially risky, Field and her colleagues fulfill theater’s highest calling: to reflect our shared humanity to us, in all its complexity and contradiction.

Monarch Butterfly on a Pink Zinnia. Photo (c)2006 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man), GFDL 1.2 <http://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/fdl-1.2.html>, via Wikimedia Commons

As the audience departed the theater, many lingered in quiet conversation, seemingly reluctant to break the spell cast by this moving production. In a theatrical landscape often dominated by escapist fare, “Remembrance” stands as a testament to the enduring power of theater to address our most profound human challenges with grace, honesty, and unexpected beauty.

This production runs approximately 70 minutes without intermission and includes an after-show Q and A. It continues at Theater for the New City through April 6. For those who have ever provided care to a loved one—or may someday face that challenge—”Remembrance” offers recognition of that harrowing journey and a compassionate affirmation that you are not alone.

title.rendered: How To Embarrass Your Immigrant Parents

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

Abby Govindan made her off-Broadway debut with her comedy special “How To Embarrass Your Immigrant Parents” at SoHo Playhouse for a 2-week run. With the springy energy of a camp counselor, Govindan delivered an hour that covered the turbulence of going viral at age 20, her time on a psych ward, why she decided to write to the KKK while impersonating a white woman, and, yes, that one time she convinced Twitter users and major news outlets that she was the creator of Emily in Paris and had written it as a joke.

As someone steeped in both Internet culture and Indian-American culture, Govindan’s material spoke to me immediately. Her observational humor is her strong suit with wry takes on everything from white boyfriends (they’d be ok if they could stop making it weird at Indian weddings) to credit card fraud (it’s really easy to do on accident). Her insights about her complicated relationship with her parents and the specific scrutiny placed on young women of the Internet were deeply considered. The show walked the line between a stand up special and an intimate diary, drawing us into the mind of a young woman in the process of understanding how to live as a comedian while surviving everything that the spotlight comes with.

The show was carefully scripted and delivered (Govindan even jokes that you can tell she did speech and debate in high school), which doesn’t leave much room for improvisation. Instead of going for a casual or conversational style, Govindan used the off-Broadway setting to create a deliberate performance. Some of the show’s best moments came from her use of visuals, including showing us real screenshots from her family groupchat. She used these moments to draw out the comedy inherent in immigrant parents and children trying to communicate across cultural and generational chasms. My favorite example of this was her dad attempting to be more expressive over text, which resulted in him responding for her request to pick up dog food with “No <3.”

Each word and moment of audience interaction felt planned, to the point of occasionally being too restrained. And yet, given the personal material of the show, I understood why. It’s not easy to talk about things like suicide and what you regret saying to your parents. It’s especially not easy if you’re Indian.

Having grown up in a South Asian household, I came to understand how colorful and potentially damning the Desi rumor mill can be. It makes many Indian people, including a lot of the people I grew up around, reluctant for their business to be aired publicly. In fact, it’s what led to many of the fights that Abby talks about in her special between the comedian and her parents. Something I deeply admired about the show was her willingness to portray these vulnerable moments with tenderness.

Rather than exploiting any rifts between her and her family for a joke, Govindan used these stories to paint an honest portrait of Indian parents trying to understand their American daughter. Any jokes that involved her loved ones were done not at their expense, but with a deep love and appreciation for their humanity. It ended up being the kind of show that will make you want to call your stoic, immigrant dad just to say you love him. “How to Embarrass Your Immigrant Parents” is brimming with love and served with the right amount of Gen Z irreverence and wit. As she continues on her global tour, I know Govindan will continue to evolve and hone the show, and I am excited to see what’s in store for her.

 

“How To Embarrass Your Immigrant Parents” ran from March 19-22 at Soho Playhouse. See Abby Govindan’s website for more tour dates.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Donmar Warehouse‘s production of Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard is now playing on this side of the pond for a limited engagement through April 27 at St. Ann’s Warehouse. This is a new version of the play, written and directed by Benedict Andrews. It brings the themes forward from their original Russian, adding in climate change, and providing modern-day parallels to the socioeconomic forces the play originally dramatized concerning class restructuring in Russia at the turn of the 20th century, laying it up against the restructuring that we’re currently experiencing in this country.

If you don’t already know the story, the narrative centers on a Russian noblewoman, Ranevskaya (Nina Hoss), who comes back to her ancestral property, renowned for its expansive cherry orchard, prior to its auction to settle outstanding debts. Despite opportunities to preserve the estate, she remains passive, ultimately allowing its purchase by Yermolai Lopakhin (Adeel Akhtar), a man whose father once served as a serf on the land. As the family departs, the sound of the cherry orchard being felled echoes in the background.

This version of the play takes place in the round with lights always on, illuminating both the stage and the audience. As the play begins, the actors come out into the playing area, walls and floors covered with carpet, taking seats around the periphery where they, like us, are now observers as well as co-conspirators in the action. At times, the audience is incorporated, as off-stage family, and inanimate objects that bring an audience inclusive bit of comedy to the action of the play. The actors also use the aisles through the audience to expand the playing area and bring the play closer to the viewers. All of this layering on, though, does not deepen the story or characterizations, but instead becomes a pleasant distraction outside of the play.

Chekov called The Cherry Orchard a comedy, and that designation has been a bone of contention through the years, with many great artists searching to find the comedy he refers to, as the tragedy is so overwhelming. Within the immense tragedy of the situation, and the character’s personal faults, comedy is hard pressed to come into play, should we laugh at Ranevskaya giving her last kopecks away? Should we laugh at the constant boredom being expressed by the characters. Should we laugh at Firs (Karl Johnson) being forgotten and boarded up in the house to die? Ha ha, the ridiculousness of the self-involved rich.

There are some characters, Yepikhodov (Eanna Hardwicke) and Charlotta (Sarah Amankwah), who are purposely written to bring comic relief, but the other characters’ disdain and unmitigated disdain of them dampens their comedic efforts. I’ve always wondered if the comedy in this play would strike a stronger chord when played to an audience in a lower demographic? But that is a hard-pressed task as the cost of doing and watching theater is not an easy hill to climb. The struggle with this production, in its quest to relevancy, modernism, and being present, is reflected in the extraneous efforts to use the audience and the playing space as an extra foil, giving voice to the fact that the action on the stage is not enough. It becomes a trying too hard to find the laugh, and if it’s not there, go outside the play and create it. Chekov is sublte. Sometimes too damn subtle.

As is with all art, what you, the audience, bring to it is on par with what the artist creates. There can be no music without ears, books without eyes, theater without an audience, or paintings without a viewer. Comedy thrives in societies experiencing shifts in power dynamics, one clinging to tradition and another pushing for progress. This production of The Cherry Orchard and what is happening in the world in 2025, mesh. Is it a tragedy, or is it a comedy? Perhaps both simultaneously.

In a Russian comedy, life is terrible, winter and darkness shall consume us, and we shall all perish, so let’s drink some vodka!

In a Russian tragedy, there is no vodka.

—–

The Cherry Orchard by Anton Chekov. Rewritten and directed by Benedict Andrews.

The cast includes Josh Adler, Adeel Akhtar (Yermolai Lopakhin), Sarah Amankwah (Charlotta Ivanovna), David Ganly (Boris Simeonov-Pischik Borisovich), Michael Gould (Leonid Gaev Andreevich), Éanna Hardwicke (Semyon Yepikhodov Panteleevich), Nina Hoss (Liubov Ranevskaya Andreevna), Karl Johnson (Firs), Daniel Monks (Pyotr Trofimov Sergeevich), Marli Siu (Varya), Sarah Slimani (Yasha), Sadie Soverall (Anya), and Posy Sterling (Dunyasha).

The creative team is Benedict Andrews (Director & Adaptor), Magda Willi (Set Designer), Merle Hensel (Costume Designer), James Farncombe (Lighting Designer), Brendan Aanes (Sound Designer, St. Ann’s Warehouse), Dan Balfour (Original Sound Designer, Donmar Warehouse), May Kershaw (Composer), Anna Cooper (Casting Director), Neetu Singh (Assistant Director), and Miguel Figueiredo (Associate Lighting Designer).
Running time is 2 hours and 45 minutes with one intermission.
Tickets for The Cherry Orchard are on sale now, $64 – $134, and can be purchased at stannswarehouse.org.

The production features haze, cigarettes, vaping, and a non-firing replica firearm.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

We forget, or I do, that reviewing a show is journalism.  It is an actual thing.  George Clooney and Grant Heslov‘s “Good Night, and Good Luck,” makes the point in spades.  Reporters report.  We reviewers are reporters, advising you to take yourself to the theatre or stay home and buy your sweetheart a hot fudge sundae.  In this case you can forgo the sundae if you have the do-re-mi.

“Good Night, and Good Luck,” is a detailed black and white account of the lead up to, and the execution of, the 1954 confrontation between The Junior Senator from Wisconsin, Joseph McCarthy and the journalist Edward R. Murrow, the host of “See It Now,” CBS’s weekly half-hour news program.  According to a feature article in the New York Times about Time Magazine’s cover story on McCarthy in 1954, McCarthy was  “… at the very height of his political power. For four years he had terrorized the nation with his wild and exaggerated charges that nearly every branch of the Government had been infiltrated by Communists and fellow travelers who were busily doing the Soviet Union’s dirty work. In the cold‐war climate of fear that the Senator was exploiting and exacerbating, the careers of many eminent men and women were being destroyed on the basis of hearsay evidence — or no evidence at all — and McCarthy’s rampage seemed unstoppable.”

Sound familiar?

Knowing how long the path to Broadway can take (years if not decades) I suppose that when this project began   it was impossible to predict the miserable situation in which we find ourselves today.  I am betting, however, that Clooney and company had an inkling based on Trump’s past behavior, if you can even call it that.  They ended up with a story whose simplicity is both an easy to follow guide as well as a challenge.

After four years of McCarthy raking an entire country over the coals, the wagons were beginning to circle up.  Murrow (Clooney) and his producer, Fred Friendly (Glenn Fleshler) kept a tight rein on the staff and reporters.  Accusations could not be based on gut hunches, no matter how sincere the source.  Proof was the coin of the realm.  Murrow was walking a fine line in terms of timing.  The attack on McCarthy had to come from Murrow before McCarthy came for him.  And it WAS coming. Murrow’s strike occurred on March 9, 1954.  That night, Murrow told his audience that the 30 minute program would be devoted to McCarthy in his own words.  Very little would be said by Murrow.  He told the viewers, “… the line between investigating and persecuting is a very fine one; and the Junior Senator from Wisconsin has stepped over it repeatedly. We must not confuse dissent with disloyalty.”

It was not the end for McCarthy, but it was the beginning of the end.

This production is impeccable.  David Cromer has succeeded in bringing this most excellent script – much of which is lifted directly from Murrow – to full bloom. The set design (Scott Pask) turns the stage into a live TV sound stage, production room, editing and news room. Each actor moves from pillar to post over and over again without pause.  The jazz combo provides soft jazz of the period (on the night I attended the singer Imani Rouselle was filling in for Georgia Heers and did a spectacular job).  The intertwining of secondary plots of secret lives widens the gates of our connection to the story.  The play’s conclusion knocks it out of the park by about a bazillion miles and takes us with it.

What is arresting, however, is watching Clooney.  Sure, sure I know he’s a movie star, and movie stars are easy eye candy.  Clooney, however, embraces Murrow completely.  He has modified his own speech patterns to emulate Murrow without a hiccup – you should pardon the expression.  (Gigi Buffington was Dialect Coach) – and oh how lovely it is to hear someone speak without an “um” or worse “LIKE” in the entire speech.  Murrow was precise, and Clooney makes us appreciate that precision.  As well, a person can almost hear both Clooney and Murrow thinking, planning, plotting the next move.  Every moment on stage is guided by some inner tracking device.  Clooney is an actor who makes it look easy.  This is a masterclass.

It is good to see a mega star, a multi-millionaire, put his money where his mouth is.  With “Good Night and Good Luck,” George Clooney does just that.

On the down side, it is too bad that the least expensive ticket, found with some digging, is $350.  Most Orchestra tickets are in the $800-900 range.  Therefore, the people to whom this story is dedicated – you know, the working stiff who just wants to do a good job – will never be able to pay the fee and experience this homage to Murrow.  They will miss out on being inspired to take action today because they don’t have $350 to spare.

This is the exact opposite of the spirit of Murrow and his own definition of his work:  “What sets me apart from Sen. McCarthy.” Ed Murrow once explained. “is my devotion to the principles upon which this nation rests—justice, freedom and fairness.”  It is not fair to have tickets that most of us cannot afford.

Like the King said – “This is a Puzzlement.” One helluva puzzlement.

PS – How about a real bow-tie for this extraordinary man?

Good Night, and Good Luck, by George Clooney and Grant Heslov. Directed by winner David Cromer

WITH Mac Brandt, George Clooney, Will Dagger, Christopher Denham, Glenn Fleshler, Ilana Glazer, Clark Gregg, Paul Gross, Georgia Heers, Carter Hudson, Fran Kranz, Jennifer Morris, Michael Nathanson, Andrew Polk, Aaron Roman Weiner, and R. Ward Duffy, Joe Forbrich, Imani Rousselle, Greg Stuhr, JD Taylor, and Sophia Tzougros rounding out the ensemble. 

The creative team for Good Night, and Good Luck includes Scott Pask (scenic design), Heather Gilbert (lighting design), David Bengali (video/projections design), Daniel Kluger (sound design), Brenda Abbandandolo (costume design), Leah J. Loukas (hair & wig design), Gigi Buffington (voice & dialect), Daniel Kluger and Bryan Carter (music supervision)

Through June 8 at the Winter Garden Theatre.  Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

Jack O’Brien’s production of Ibsen’s Ghosts at Lincoln Center’s Newhouse Theater begins with a baffling choice. The cast enters holding scripts, mumbling inaudibly as if in rehearsal, only to suddenly exit, discard their folders, and return to “actually” begin the play. The gesture reappears only at curtain call, when the cast returns with the same folders in hand. Neither of these moments accomplish anything.

Ghosts is a study in quiet devastation. The past unravels and collides with the present in violent and horrific ways. It requires steadiness, restraint, perhaps even minimalism. It has the tone of a Caravaggio or Van Dyck painting. But O’Brien overlays the work with extraneous choices that distance us from the story. The costuming is modern (though partial, inconsistent, and inconsequential), as is the speech (via this new version by Mark O’Rowe). In performance, actors twitch and shriek.

Only Lily Rabe, as Mrs. Alving, seems to understand what the story requires. She stands straight. She speaks directly. Her presence is quiet but weighted. Even her throaty voice seems to carry a painful past. In small moments—a pause, then a simple “Ah”—she captures a woman who once fled her marriage only to be persuaded to return, a decision that has haunted her life.

That performance should find its dramatic counterweight in Pastor Manders, played by Billy Crudup. But, oh boy, it doesn’t. There should be a battle of ideas and ideals between the two, especially given their implied romantic past—a crucial tension that collapses with Crudup’s performance. This ideological conflict is a vital engine in the play, yet Crudup (yes, a Tony winner) all but extinguishes it. He’s frantic and fidgety where Manders requires rigidity. He bends his back, jerks his head, flails his hands, and squeaks. These movements suggest less a man of God and more the Los Pollos Hermanos mascot.

Ella Beatty, as Regina (the Alvings’ maid), suffers from similar problems. Her speech is unmodulated and unconvincing. Regina is a maid raised in deference, yet Beatty plays her with brazenness, almost as if no class distinction exists. Hamish Linklater, in contrast, delivers a compelling Engstrand (Regina’s adoptive father). He shows us sorrow and desperation, bringing emotional depth and a naïveté that wins laughs.

Levon Hawke gives a serviceable Oswald, Mrs. Alving’s son. While not delivering a performance for the ages in this classic role, he successfully communicates the story and rises to the challenge of the play’s final, excruciating scene with Rabe—a moment that demands bravery from both actors. They deliver it, and powerfully so.

One can’t help but note the casting’s ironic resonance with the play’s theme of inheritance. Levon Hawke (son of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman), Ella Beatty (daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening), Lily Rabe (daughter of playwright David Rabe), and Hamish Linklater (son of legendary vocal teacher Kristin Linklater) form a roster of theatrical heirs. In a play where Oswald inherits syphilis and Regina a life of service, we watch the offspring of Hollywood royalty inherit their parents’ profession. Was this intentional?

There are moments where Ibsen breaks through. His play is too strong not to. That final scene between mother and son remains staggering. Ghosts influenced generations of playwrights. It was a turning point in modern drama. And so, despite everything, watching Ghosts remains an affecting experience. The force of the story, the tragedy that emerges from societal constraints and past decisions, is still there. Some plays are so deeply rooted in human experience, so exact in their dramatic construction, that they survive their interpreters.

Ghosts is one of them.

GHOSTS by Henrik Ibsen; Directed by Jack O’Brien.

With: Ella Beatty, Billy Crudup, Levon Hawke, Hamish Linklater, and Lily Rabe.

Sets by John Lee Beatty. Costumes by Jess Goldstein. Original Music by Mark Bennett. Sound by Scott Lehrer and Mark Bennett.

Now playing through April 26 at Lincoln Center, Mitzi E. Newhouse Theater, 150 W 65th St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 110 minutes, no intermission.

excerpt.rendered: O’Brien’s production buries Ibsen’s haunted restraint under some weak performances and extraneous choices—but Ghosts is too strong a play to be undone completely.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Masterclass is closing out its worldwide victory lap, having won the hearts, minds, and patriarchy bashing distortions of the current world order.

Defying any theatrical categorization, Masterclass starts off as a farcical mimicry of a televised interview (two chairs, coffee table, fake fig leaf plants) by 70s costumed Feidlim Cannon, of the mad theatrical genius, Truscott, and his misogynistic writing and work. Saying his work is all about truth,  but then confronted by his backstage dalliances, the truth becomes, not unsurprisingly, murky. Dismissing his white/male race and sex privilege for his notoriety, he sits on the altar of his anointed genius, indulgently passing judgment as he looks down from his perch, gun in hand. His attempts at suicide seem to elicit effect more than any true sympathies. His comparison to Hemingway, at one point, only seems to stoke his fires of self-indulgency. It’s jumbled craziness exposing societally imposed white male privilege.

This interview send-up of the great white male artist replete with body padding, wigs, fake mustache, and buffoonery is quirky, absurd, and eventually tumbles upon itself to a full stop. What emerges from that pile of insanity is another stark truth, a more direct and current dissection of male-focused western art and the detrimental consequences of its power. Performer Adrienne Truscott sheds her skin, becomes herself, and dives into the painful truths of art and gender. Theatricality takes a backseat, and the search for personal truth comes on display as Adrienne and Feidlim examine their singular truths and challenge each other’s blinders.

If you consider yourself a deep thinker and very interested in artistic and cultural hierarchy and how changing it could alter our whole societal landscape, this show might be for you. For myself, I love it when theater challenges me.

Masterclass is performed by Adrienne Truscott and Brokentalkers Co-Artistic Director Feidlim Cannon.

Their last remaining shows in the States will play the Fisher Center at Bard College, April 3 – 6. $40 Tickets can be purchased HERE.

I want to also send a shout out to NYU Skirball and the programming that they consistently put together. Everything, and yes, I mean everything, that they present is challenging, surprising, thought-provoking, and well worth experiencing. In this day and age where theater tickets can now be in the four figures, it’s nice to know you will be transported, entertained, and challenged at an affordable price.
