title.rendered: Leonkoro String Quartet: Sublime Brilliance at the 92nd Street Y

content.rendered:
The Leonkoro Quartet presented a transcendent evening of chamber music mastery. In the intimate acoustical jewel of Buttenwieser Hall at the Arnhold Center, the Leonkoro String Quartet delivered a performance of such breathtaking virtuosity and emotional depth that time seemed suspended. The concert on March 29 traversed three centuries of chamber music with astonishing technical precision and interpretive maturity that belied the ensemble’s relatively recent formation in 2019.

The String Quartet is Authentic and Miraculous

Music written for a string quartet is special. A superb ensemble like the Leonkoro Quartet performing quartet masterpieces is miraculous! I’ll explain.

Unlike a symphony’s grandeur or a concerto’s lushness, the quartet is intimate. Thriving in small halls and private salons, the audience hears the breathing, the scraping of bows, and the sighs of each phrase. Composers often use the form to express their most personal, unfiltered thoughts.

Spiritual Reflection through Music

Beethoven’s Heiliger Dankgesang in Op. 132, for example, is a deeply spiritual reflection on his recovery from illness. Bartók’s string quartets trace a journey through dissonance, folk music, and modernism. Schubert’s Death and the Maiden quartet is haunted by mortality. These are not works of public display—they are confessions.

Here’s a sample of the Leonkoro Quartet performing Puccini’s heartfelt “Crisantemi”:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Leonkoro Quartet (@leonkoroquartet)

The Leonkoro Quartet: Young Lions with Veteran Hearts

From the opening notes of Caroline Shaw‘s “Entr’acte,” it was immediately apparent that listeners were experiencing a string quartet of exceptional caliber. The Leonkoro Quartet—whose name appropriately derives from the Esperanto for “lionheart”—performed while standing (except for cellist Lukas Schwarz), creating a visual fluidity mirroring their musical flexibility. This physical approach enhanced their already remarkable communication and dynamic cohesion.

First violinist Jonathan Schwarz led with aristocratic poise and searing intensity, drawing a spectrum of colors from his instrument. His brother Lukas anchored the ensemble with a cello tone of extraordinary warmth and resonance. Second violinist Amelie Wallner displayed remarkable versatility, alternately supporting and emerging from the texture with impeccable judgment. Meanwhile, violist Mayu Konoe provided the crucial inner voice with eloquent expression and technical brilliance.

Jonathan Schwarz, Violin and Amelie Wallner, Violin. Courtesy leonkoroquartet.com

Shaw’s “Entr’acte”: Contemporary Magic Through Classical Inspiration

The Leonkoro Quartet approached Caroline Shaw’s “Entr’acte” with a kaleidoscopic range of sounds and techniques. Written in 2011 and inspired by Haydn’s String Quartet in F Major, Shaw’s piece reimagines the classical minuet and trio form through a contemporary prism. The quartet masterfully navigated its technical demands, including virtuosic left-hand pizzicato, eerie sul ponticello effects, and delicate harmonics.

Moreover, the ensemble’s impeccable control of dynamics brought Shaw’s subtle phrases to life with crystalline clarity. The work’s dénouement featured Schwarz’s cello executing triple stops in a pizzicato style reminiscent of a harp or guitar—a moment of transfixing beauty rendered with consummate skill.

Paul Hindemith in the USA (1939-40). See page for author, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

Hindemith’s Wartime Masterpiece: Leonkoro Quartet Scales Dramatic Heights

Paul Hindemith’s String Quartet No. 2 in F Minor emerged as the evening’s dramatic centerpiece. Composed during World War I while the 22-year-old Hindemith served as a military sentry, this powerful work received a reading of extraordinary intensity from the Leonkoro Quartet. The ensemble displayed their extensive dramatic range in hushed, mysterious passages or moments of lush romantic expression.

The quartet navigated the first movement’s ghostly fugue with spectral precision. Subsequently, they brought wit and character to the variations movement, honoring Hindemith’s blend of tradition and innovation. The waltz variation lilted gracefully while the scherzo passages sparkled with brilliant virtuosity. Each quartet member projected a rich, expressive presence throughout this musical powerhouse.

In the finale’s fast, furious sections, the ensemble continued to demonstrate their flawless technique and superb ensemble skills. Furthermore, they honored Hindemith’s artistic intent with remarkable fidelity, bringing his war-born masterpiece to vivid life. Most impressively, the young quartet displayed virtuosity and the maturity to sustain lengthy musical passages of profound depth and character.

Mayu Konoe, Viola and Lucas Schwarz, Cello. Courtesy leonkoroquartet.com

Beethoven’s Late Masterwork: The Summit of String Quartet Writing

After intermission, the Leonkoro Quartet tackled Beethoven’s monumental String Quartet No. 15 in A Minor, Op. 132, with the same exceptional skill and insight they had brought to the earlier works. This late-period masterpiece, composed during Beethoven’s convalescence in 1825, received an interpretation of sublime brilliance and spiritual depth.

The quartet’s communication on stage approached telepathy, ensuring the most subtle passages were executed with perfect precision—their approach to Beethoven’s complex opening movement balanced intellectual rigor with emotional intensity. The second movement flowed with elegant restraint, preparing the audience for the profound heart of the work.

“Heiliger Dankgesang”: A Sacred Musical Offering

The central movement, “Heiliger Dankgesang eines Genesenen an die Gottheit” (Holy Song of Thanksgiving from a Convalescent to the Divinity), revealed the Leonkoro Quartet’s exceptional capacity for sustained spiritual expression. This extended movement—Beethoven’s gratitude for recovery from serious illness—unfolded with transcendent beauty.

The ensemble rendered the Lydian mode sections with a luminous transparency that seemed to lift the music toward the divine. Subsequently, the contrasting “feeling new strength” sections brought gentle vitality before returning to contemplation. The quartet’s sensitivity to the music and each other’s subtle inflections was extraordinary.

The march and finale received equally magnificent treatment. The ensemble navigated Beethoven’s ambiguous emotional terrain with remarkable insight. Their approach to this ambitious, glorious, and angelic music honored Beethoven’s genius with technical aplomb and profound understanding.

Portret van Ludwig van Beethoven. Public Domain

Three Masterworks: A Timeline of Chamber Music Evolution

This carefully constructed program illuminated the evolution of the string quartet from Beethoven’s transcendent late period to our contemporary moment. Beethoven’s Op. 132, composed when completely deaf, pushed the boundaries of chamber music into previously unimaginable realms of expression. Nearly a century later, Hindemith—a violist and quartet performer—crafted his F Minor quartet while surviving the trenches of World War I.

Caroline Shaw, whose “Entr’acte” opened the program, represents the quartet’s vibrant present and future. Inspired directly by Haydn (the form’s originator) but employing contemporary techniques, Shaw connects a 250-year tradition to our current musical language. This brilliant programming by the Leonkoro Quartet illuminated the string quartet’s remarkable journey through musical history.

Buttenwieser Hall: A Perfect Setting for Chamber Music Intimacy

The 92nd Street Y’s Buttenwieser Hall at the Arnhold Center provided an ideal acoustic environment for this extraordinary performance. The warm, intimate space allowed whispered pianissimos and forceful fortissimos to register with perfect clarity. Furthermore, its excellent sight lines created an immersive experience where audience members could observe the quartet’s subtle visual communication.

This historic venue has long been one of New York’s premier chamber music destinations. Indeed, its legacy includes performances by legendary ensembles from the Budapest Quartet to the Emerson. The Leonkoro Quartet now joins this illustrious lineage, having conquered the hall with their exceptional artistry.

The post-concert reception in Buttenwieser Lounge offered a delightful opportunity for audience members to discuss the revelatory performance they had just experienced. Many lingered, clearly reluctant for such a magical evening to end. The Leonkoro Quartet had delivered not merely a concert but a profound musical communion.

As this extraordinary young ensemble continues its first North American tour, music lovers in Boston, Montreal, Chicago, Houston, and San Francisco have transformative experiences awaiting them. Based on this triumphant New York debut, their ascent to the highest echelon of international chamber ensembles seems not just likely but inevitable. Click the next photo for information about their current tour.

Leonkoro Quartet. L-R: Lukas Schwarz, Cello, Jonathan Schwarz, Violin, Mayu Konoe, Viola, and Amelie Wallner, Violin. Courtesy leonkoroquartet.com

 

The 92ND Street Y

Theresa L. Kaufman Concert Hall
The 92nd Street Y, New York
1395 Lexington Avenue
(between 91st & 92nd street)
New York, NY 10128

For tickets and information on the current Concert Season, visit www.92NY.org.

Readers may also enjoy High Octane Octet: The ACO at Weill Recital Hall, and Tapping into the Twenties: The ASO and Forgotten Marvels at David Geffen Hall.

title.rendered: High Octane Octet: The ACO at Weill Recital Hall

content.rendered:
In the hallowed acoustic sanctuary of Carnegie Hall’s Weill Recital Hall, the American Classical Orchestra celebrated its 40th anniversary with a transformational performance. The High Octane Octet program, presented on March 28, combined remarkable musicianship with period-authentic instruments to create an evening of rare musical splendor. This milestone celebration showcased why ACO remains one of America’s most vital classical ensembles.

Period Instruments and the Magic of Gut Strings: The High Octane Octet Experience

The evening’s centerpiece, Mendelssohn’s brilliant Octet in E-flat Major, dazzled with youthful exuberance. Moreover, the musicians’ 19th-century instruments provided a sublime tonal palette that modern setups cannot replicate. The gut strings, standard in Mendelssohn’s time, produced a warm, textured sound with remarkable clarity across the dynamic spectrum. Consequently, audiences experienced something extraordinary—the music as Mendelssohn himself would have heard it performed nearly 200 years ago.

Crawford’s Illuminating Introduction: The Architectural Genius of Mendelssohn

Before the performance, Maestro Thomas Crawford, ACO’s founder and artistic director, offered a fascinating exploration of Mendelssohn’s compositional techniques. Crawford’s avuncular wit and encyclopedic knowledge transformed what could have been a dry analysis into an engaging musical journey. With violinist Edson Scheid expertly demonstrating key themes, Crawford enthusiastically revealed the octet’s intricate architecture.

The audience chuckled warmly as Crawford recounted the orchestra’s early collaborations with unlikely partners. His anecdotes about Christopher Reeves, Conan O’Brien, and ultimately weathercaster Al Roker, who narrated a children’s concert, highlighted ACO’s commitment to bringing classical music to new audiences. These personal touches humanized the evening, creating an intimate connection between performers and listeners.

High Octane Octet – the ACO in Carnegie Hall’s Weill Recital Hall. Courtesy aconyc.org

Sonata Form and Romantic Innovation: Inside the High Octane Octet

Crawford’s detailed examination of the octet’s movements, each organized in sonata form, revealed Mendelssohn’s compositional mastery. He illuminated how the composer, like Beethoven before him, employed arpeggios to craft memorable themes of astonishing emotional power. Furthermore, he highlighted the octet’s scherzo—a movement of virtuosic gossamer lightness that would later influence generations of composers.

Here is the delightful theme of the opening of the Octet demonstrating Mendelssohn’s use of arpeggio figures.

Dvořák’s Miniatures: Pathos in Brief Elegance

The evening began with Dvořák’s charming Miniatures, Op. 75a, performed with exquisite sensitivity by violinists Edson Scheid and Karl Kawahara, joined by violist David Cerutti. This trio, composed initially for an amateur student, revealed Dvořák’s gift for creating profound emotional landscapes within compact musical forms. The High Octane Octet program demonstrated how these miniatures portray the same pathos and Czech folk influence that characterize Dvořák’s larger chamber works.

The Cavatina’s gentle lyricism flowed beautifully under Scheid’s assured leadership. Subsequently, the spirited Capriccio danced with Bohemian rhythmic vitality. The Romance, with its dreamy melodic contours, showcased the ensemble’s perfect balance, while the elegiac final movement achieved a haunting beauty that belied its brevity.

Felix Mendelssohn’s Leipzig study. Public Domain

Virtuosic Ensemble: The Stars of High Octane Octet

The octet performance featured a stellar assembly of period instrument specialists. First violinist Krista Bennion Feeney led with aristocratic poise, her 19th-century violin producing tones of honeyed warmth. Meanwhile, Karl Kawahara, Theresa Salomon, and Edson Scheid completed the violin section with technical brilliance and stylistic cohesion.

Violists David Cerutti and Annie Garlid provided a rich middle voice, their gut-strung instruments offering a distinctively husky timbre unavailable on modern instruments. Cellists Myron Lutzke and Serafim Smigelskiy anchored the ensemble with profoundly resonant bass lines, creating a solid and flexible foundation.

The American Classical Orchestra: Champions of Authentic Sound

Under Crawford’s visionary leadership, the ACO has spent four decades championing historically informed performances on period instruments. This High Octane Octet program exemplified the orchestra’s mission—revealing masterworks’ original colors and textures through meticulous attention to historical performance practices. Their commitment to gut strings, classical bows, and appropriate playing techniques creates sonic landscapes of astonishing authenticity.

Crawford’s scholarly approach never comes at the expense of emotional impact. Instead, the historical techniques serve the music’s expressive essence. The ACO consistently demonstrates that period performance isn’t merely academic— it is a vibrant, living tradition that brings familiar works into sharper focus.

Antonin Dvořák. Public Domain.

Historical Context: The Legacy of Chamber Music Masterworks

Both works on the program represent pivotal moments in chamber music history. Mendelssohn’s octet, composed at 16, virtually invented a new genre—eight string players performing as a unified ensemble rather than as separate quartets. Furthermore, its symphonic approach influenced chamber writing for generations.

Dvořák’s Miniatures, though less monumental, showcases the composer’s unique gift for expressing profound emotions through simple means. Originally written for an amateur student, these pieces demonstrate how accessibility and artistic excellence coexist. Both compositions continue to inspire performers and composers today through their perfect marriage of form and expression.

Weill Recital Hall: The Perfect Setting for High Octane Octet

With its gilded elegance and impeccable acoustics, Carnegie Hall’s intimate Weill Recital Hall provided the ideal setting for this chamber music celebration. The 268-seat jewel box venue opened in 1891 and has hosted the world’s most excellent chamber musicians for over a century. Its warm, embracing acoustics allowed every nuance of the gut-strung instruments to project with crystalline clarity.

The hall’s neoclassical beauty and cream and gold décor complemented the evening’s refined musical offerings. Light glinted off the instruments’ burnished surfaces as the music filled the space without amplification or electronic enhancement. This acoustic purity ideally suited ACO’s commitment to authentic sound production.

A Transcendent Musical Journey

As the Mendelssohn octet reached its exuberant finale, the audience experienced that rare moment when time seemed suspended. The High Octane Octet performance had transcended mere entertainment to become something genuinely profound—a communion with musical greatness across centuries. Crawford and his magnificent musicians delivered a concert and a musical revelation.

The American Classical Orchestra’s 40th anniversary season continues on May 7 with “Magnificently Mozart” at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall. Based on this triumphant High Octane Octet performance, classical music lovers would be wise to secure tickets immediately.

American Classical Orchestra

PO Box 366 New York
NY 10025-0007
Office: (212) 362-2727

For tickets and information, go to https://aconyc.org/.

Readers may also enjoy  American Classical Orchestra (ACO) and Chorus performing J. S. Bach’s St. John Passion and the American Classical Orchestra presents Astronomical.

content.rendered:
by Margret Echeverria

I gotta tell you two things straight up: this show is perfect and right now is the perfect time for us to see it.  The new musical Buena Vista Social Club, written by Marco Ramirez, developed and directed by Saheem Ali, is now playing at the Shoenfeld Theatre.  In 1996, Ry Cooder brought together legendary Cuban musicians, many of whom had left public life shortly after the revolution in 1959, to record music that was playful Cuban tradition wrapped around lyrics from hearts aching with loss and yearning for freedom.   Today, this new muscial tells a story inspired by some genuine historical truth woven into what “feels like truth” playing inside poetry.

The sensual choreography by Patricia Delgado and Justin Peck has dancers flowing into one another on the stage like lovers.  Many audience members sway in their seats awakened to a cast truly enjoying themselves.  Juan De Marcos (Justin Cunningham) a character inspired by Cooder, arrives in Cuba to record “a love letter to the Golden Age of Cuban Music.” He is daring to convince Omara (Natalie Venetia Belcon) to lend her voice to the project.  Omara arrives at a modern Havana studio where old friends, collaborators she knew 40 years ago, are very pleased to see her.  This reunion is marked by a sense that these gentle humans have survived something very painful.  We look back to winter, 1958, in Havana.  Two sisters, Young Omara (Isa Antonetti) and Young Haydee (Ashley De La Rosa), known as the Songbirds of Havana, are preparing just a few days before New Year’s Eve to sing at the Tropicana as part of the holiday celebrations.  Americans from Capitol Records will be there that night and Young Haydee is sure they will be offered a contract.  But Young Omara’s world opens when new friends introduce her to the Buena Vista Social Club.  The club is on the “wrong” side of town and Young Haydee has some harsh judgments tinged with racism and classism about being seen at Buena Vista.  Young Omara, however, feels totally at home at the club loving the freedom she has to sing exactly as she wants to sing.  Antonetti’s voice is an absolute star.  The mysteries of her heart spill raw from her tongue.  It’s clear Young Omara would rather sing at the Buena Vista Social Club than at the Tropicana.

Isa Antonetti in Buena Vista Social Club photo by Matthew Murphy

But the world outside Young Omara’s experience is about to explode.  New Year’s Eve 1958 in Havana is the night Castro’s revolutionaries violently drive out Batista’s regime and take over Cuba.  Does Young Omara want to leave Havana for New York and a music contract or stay in Cuba where her future is now completely uncertain?  The horrors of that night force the young women to make practical decisions very quickly in excruciating circumstances.  The acting chops in these singers and dancers is fluid.  I was with them; empathizing because, overwhelmed by pain in the last two months here in the U.S., I feel and witness similar stiffened resolve to not wallow, but act.  Young Omara decides to stay in Havana as Young Haydee narrowly escapes before Cuba is completely shut down.  And I’m crying.

We’re brought forward again to Juan De Marcos’ rented studio, where Belcon’s mature Omara works an emotional arc through the progression of her songs, which ache with longing, reflect her losses, and then bring glorious hope alive.

This cast of supporting characters give us many moments of pure delight.  Eliades (Renesito Avich), the troubadour and incredible guitar player, has an adorable face and irrisistible humour, but Avich steals the show at the top of the second act leaving us breathless with fast fingering and impossible harmonics.  Compay (Julio Monge) is the friend you just might be lucky enough to have in your life.  He is ready with a story, a quip and profound wisdom that vibrates in perfect pitch on the right beat.  Monge’s comic timing and endearing physicality had me in tears of true love.  Young Ibrahim (Wesley Wray), Young Omara’s handsome love interest, is a character who inspires Young Omara to be true to her artistry over being subservient to him.  I love that Ramirez’s writing does not diminish Omara’s heroism with a dependance on a man.  Rather, he sets her free.  And Wray is utterly surrendered to her as he sings complex close harmonies with Antonetti that make us swoon.

As we lie awake tonight, many of us will wonder if the US is headed for a revolution.  Cuba and the gift of the Buena Vista Social Club remind us that art made with love can ground us, heal us, unite us and maybe just save us all.

BUENA VISTA SOCIAL CLUB, book by Marco Ramirez, songs by Buena Vista Social Club, directed by Saheem Ali.

WITH Natalie Venetia Belcon (Omara), Julio Monge (Compay), Mel Semé (Ibrahim), Jainardo Batista Sterling (Rubén), Isa Antonetti (Young Omara), Da’von Moody (Young Compay), Wesley Wray (Young Ibrahim), Leonardo Reyna (Young Rubén), Renesito Avich (Eliades), Ashley De La Rosa (Young Haydee), Justin Cunningham (Juan de Marcos); and band — Marco Paguia (piano, music direction), guitarist David Oquendo, Gustavo Schartz (guitar), Hery Paz (woodwinds), Eddie Venegas (trombone), Jesus Ricardo (trumpet), Javier Díaz, Mauricio Herrera, and Román Diaz (percussion)

Choreography by Justin Peck and Patricia Delgado, sets by Arnulfo Maldonado, costumes by Dede Ayite, lighting by Tyler Micoleau, sound by Jonathan Deans.

Runs through January 4, 2026.  Gerald Shoenfeld Theatre, 236 W 45th St New York, NY.  Get tix here.  Run time 2 hours 15 minutes (includes 15 minute intermission).

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Every time I see Charles Busch perform I realize that I am exactly where i want to be.  In his audience. Busch has that effect on people.  He pulls us in.  It is no accident.  It is magic that he has crafted over the decades.

As Busch talks we can feel him But marveling at the world and his place in it.  His stories are more of a casual travel-log that filled with enchanting pit stops, and each song is cocooned with a story – like the time he discovered Billy Holiday’s accompanist working as a janitor at the Children’s Center in New  York.  The teenage Busch found a piano and the two had more than one session.  His “Crazy He Calls Me” (Carl Sigman/Bob Russell) delivered after the story blossoms in the new light of a decades old tale.

A note about the band: Busch has assembled an eclectic mix that is perfectly balanced.  Kim Bonsanti (trumpet) adds a note of smooth nostalgia in her new life as a retired cop returning to music.  John Miller (bass and also Busch’s cousin) provides the lush foundation for the evening.  Loic Da Silva is a multilingual accordion player who ads just the right spice.  Jono Mainelli is an elegant, and funny Music Director who pulls the evening together.

Over the years, Busch has charted his own path over and over again.  An interest in dialect led him to a class at Northwestern where he heard a classmate recite “Pirate Jenny” (Kurt Weill/Bertolt Brecht).  He was blown away and made it his business to get him thither to the library where he found the record and changed his life by listening to it.  This is the story that infuses his own rendition of same.  It is an homage to the people watching us watching them.  Perfect for New Yorkers.

The thing about Busch’s stories is that they are not filler.  They are real and enviable. There is the story about Bette Midler‘s first album (I have mine still) and the unimaginable life twist that made them friends.  Busch’s nephew, the very talented Jimmy Stull, brought his considerable guitar chops to augment the tragedy that is “Superstar” (on that same album – you know the one we all remember).  It is a sublime duet.

That same album inspired Busch to go to the record store and buy an Andrews Sisters album.  Years later he appeared onstage with Maxine Andrews.  This leads us into the boogie-woogie number “Beat Me Daddy, Eight To The Bar” (Don Raye, Hughie Prince and Ray McKinley) – with harmonies by Mainelli and Busch and some delicious trumpet licks provided by Bonsanti.

When asked to be part of a tribute to Joni Mitchell, Busch was given “Both Sides Now,’ and as is his wont, he dove in to the text and discovered that this is a song that gives itself to an examination of life – especially when you have a few years under your belt.  Were the choices really choices?  Or were they illusions?  How to know?  Perhaps surrender is, indeed, the best action.

The greatest show about actresses is “Follies” and the greatest songs about actresses are from “Follies”.  Years ago, Busch was invited to the Rainbow Room as the annual one male guest at the Women of the Theatre Luncheon.  At that time he was traveling in drag.  The suit he chose had not been worn in while and it turned out the skirt was more snug than he remembered.  He did his best to camouflage the condition, and was called out by none other than Elaine Stritch (after she told him his speech was brilliant and that she was in love – with him).  “I’m Still Here” (Stephen Sondheim)  is an homage to Stritch.  It is brilliant, sprinkled with anecdotes, and hilarious.  Roof officially blown off the place.

He closes with “Don’t Like Goodbyes,” (Harold Arlen and Truman Capote) which is his way of telling us we have to leave.  After one more story of course, the one featuring Patti LaBelle.  He leaves us better than he found us, and there is not a dry thigh in the house.  Not one.

A brilliant, rich evening.  And I was exactly where I wanted to be once again.

March 21-23, 2025 at 54 Below

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

By Tulis McCall

When you leave the Music Box Theatre after witnessing “The Picture Of Dorian Gray,” I challenge you to define what you have seen.  Theatre – of course, because it is an event taking place on a stage in the most brightly lit corner of the building.  What else?  A marathon.  A marathon at the center of which is one actor, Sarah Snook,  surrounded by 15 (count ’em) camera operators only five of which are named in the program (clew, Luka Cain, Natalie Rich, Benjamin Sheen, Dara Woo).  This means there are 10 people unaccounted for.  This unaccounting is unfortunate because without these additional 10 people there would be no show.  They do appear at the curtain call, as well they should.

The story of Dorian Gray begins with Ms. Snook upstage behind an enormous video screen.  As the Narrator, Snook is deliberate and steady, easily sliding into the first three characters we encounter: Basil who has painted the portrait, Lord Henry, who is a laconic admirer of the painting and curious about its subject, and Dorian Gray himself.

It is Henry who will draw Gray in by the power of his charm.  Snook, aided by both the camera operators and additional prerecorded video, assumes each of the many upcoming roles as if she were slipping into a new costume, which also happens as we watch.  Because of Lord Henry, Gray makes the declaration that life would be grand if he could retain the age and purity of the portrait and let the portrait assume the mortal aging that must come.

We all know what happens next.  Gray gets his wish.

And it is at this moment, when Gray realizes the wish is now reality and the portrait is aging, that the story begins to stall out like a train pulling into the station. All that is left of the roughly 40 remaining minutes is to watch Gray lose his mind in a sea of lies and debauchery. We watch as madness overcomes him like a rock concert gone off the rails.

Sarah Snook; Photo by Marc Brenner

There are dozens of surprises with camera/video work (even an iPhone gets a chance to shine) involving distortions, multiple screens appearing out of nowhere and transforming historical portraits – all amazing and somewhat distracting.  They take us away from the fact that little is happening with the story itself.  Look at us they seem to say – we are magic.  And they are.

What does not slow down one iota is Snook’s energy that never flags until the final sad moments when Gray deflates.  It is almost exhausting to watch her keep on keeping on.  We expect her to keel over at any moment.  She does not.  In addition, her commitment to Gray’s journey never waivers, and her attention to detail and specificity is off the charts.  She is a spectacular actor whose work is impeccable.

Myself – Kip Williams’ adaptation evolved into words, words, words – said Eliza Doolittle – with no silence or action to separate them. I could have used a bit of that earlier modulation that greeted us in the beginning.  In addition, an easy 30 minutes could be removed without losing any of the tale. Gray’s madness reaches such a sustained pitch that, while Snook maintains her elevation, the rest of us are left behind.  It is too much of a muchness after a while.

A mention here of the camera operators.   While Snook is the main event, and onstage the entire two hours, the camera operators are performing a ballet.  They carry cameras, they wheel tripods, they move set pieces, they carry costumes and wigs for changing and assist in said changes.   Like I said – without them there would be no show.

I wonder how many unions they had to join for this production?

Consider this the Minority Report because the audience rose to its feet with a roar at the curtain call.  I suspect it was less for the adaptation than it was for Snook and the camera operators themselves.  It was an spectacle.  It definitely was that.  I will be thinking on this one for some time to come.

 

The Picture of Dorian Gray, by Oscar Wilde; A New Adaptation written and directed by Kip Williams

WITH Sarah Snook and Camera Operators clew, Luka Cain, Natalie Rich, Benjamin Sheen, Dara Woo

Set and Costume Design is by Marg Horwell, Lighting Design by Nick Schlieper, Composition & Sound Design by Clemence Williams, Video Design by David Bergman

At The Music Box Theatre through June 15.  Running time 2 hours with no intermission. Tickets HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

By Yuval Jonas

Cold Water, by Philippa Lawford, premiered last year at the Park Theatre in London and has now been transported across the Atlantic by a new production company, Little Engine Theater. Co-founded by Lilly Englert, Theodora Miranne, and Elena Rusconi, the company’s aim is to launch international plays in New York and in “unconventional spaces.” Indeed, integral to the evening is the setting: the Ki Smith Gallery.

Upon entering, you’re drawn into a world many imagine, or perhaps hope, New York City to be: live music, art, free-flowing alcohol, and beautiful people, with accents from near and far. The atmosphere feels curated, intentional but unforced, an artful prelude to the play. On this particular evening, cellist Laura Wolf plays amidst an exhibition by photographer Bobby Grossman that features Shepard Fairey and John Holmstrom. (The musical act preceding the show changes with each performance.)

Soon, everyone heads downstairs. The basement walls are lined with more of Grossman’s work, this time stark black-and-white photographs of legendary figures that loom over the performance. The feeling is something between an underground concert and an intimate salon, but soon, indeed, it’s a play.

Cold Water takes place in the drama studio of a secondary school in Harpenden, England. At its center is Emma (Stefania LaVie Owen), a 22-year-old assistant teacher who is all ambition. For her, the job is temporary—she’s determined to get into a prestigious London drama school (well, RADA) and convinced that acting is “the only thing” she wants to do.

Her boss Matt (Ben Rosenfield) once shared the same dream. A RADA graduate himself, he had a brief, unremarkable acting career before settling into teaching. The irony isn’t lost: here’s someone who took the path Emma dreams of, only to end up in the place she’s trying to escape.

As Matt and Emma work on a student production of The Seagull, their relationship evolves from mentorship to friendship and for Emma, into something more uncertain. Matt helps Emma prepare her audition monologue for drama schools: Konstantin’s “She loves me, she loves me not.” When she delivers it, you immediately think: Why wouldn’t RADA accept her?

Owen portrays Emma with sharp comedic timing and with authenticity. Much of the play’s power comes from director Michael Herwitz’s restraint. A good deal of the time, Emma and Matt simply stand facing each other, their rapid exchanges (Stichomythia, to use my theater knowledge) punctuated by well-placed silences, beats, pauses, and breaths. In a neat act of mirroring, they teach their students the very techniques they’re using themselves.

Matt introduces Emma to his famous former RADA classmate, now a successful actor and TV producer. Suddenly, Emma is presented with real opportunities: a potential TV role and a tangible path to drama school. But as the play progresses, it becomes clear that Cold Water is not a story of triumph.

One of the most moving moments comes when Emma and Matt slip into performing the final scene between Konstantin and Nina from The Seagull. The transition is dreamlike, and suddenly, the parallels between Chekhov’s ideas—longing, failure, and artistic disillusionment—and Emma’s own aspirations hit with unexpected force.

This is also not a story about grand romance or ambition realized. It’s about the fleeting relationships that shape us—the mentors, the momentary crushes, the people who, in our brief time with them, shape who we are. For Emma, Matt will become a memory—a small pang of recollection when she passes through that town again or sees a school show. A reminder of something that once was, just for a moment. Will Emma make it? It doesn’t matter; what matters is what happens along the way.

Little Engine Theater, with their first production, prove they know what they’re doing. They’ve produced not just a play, but an experience that delivers the New York so many imagine but so few actually find. If this is their overture, the theatrical landscape of the city has gained something worth watching.

COLD WATER by Philippa Lawford; Directed by Michael Herwitz.

With: Stefania LaVie Owen and Ben Rosenfield.

Sets by Mextly Couzin. Costumes by Verity Azario. Original Music by Julia Bailen. Sound Design by Ryan Gamblin.

Now playing through April 9 at Ki Smith Gallery, 170 Forsyth St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 65 minutes, no intermission.

content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

We Had a World, Joshua Harmon’s new play on Manhattan Theatre Club’s second stage, bears a strong resemblance to another show currently running off-Broadway, Bess Wohl’s Liberation at Roundabout. Each is what Tennessee Williams coined in The Glass Menagerie—“a memory play.” But while The Glass Menagerie and Liberation focus on the ‘play’, Harmon emphasizes, perhaps too much, the ‘memory.’

Like in Liberation, the protagonist, a playwright, constructs his play onstage as he goes, and this is the play we’re watching. (Quite a Charlie Kaufman-esque metatheatrical device.) Harmon isn’t shy about the autobiographical nature of the piece. The playwright is named Joshua. At one point he’s in rehearsals for Skintight, Harmon’s own 2018 play. The link between life and art is explicit—and central.

Joshua (Andrew Barth Feldman) guides us through his relationship with his grandmother Renee (Joanna Gleason), who is now 93 and dying from cancer. He returns to scenes from his childhood, where Renee played a defining role in nurturing his curiosity and passion for the arts. She’s witty, irreverent, unapologetic (at one moment she quips, “I hope climate change happens. Winter is treacherous for people my age”). She takes him to things his mother deems inappropriate, like Dances With Wolves (with Kevin Costner’s behind), and a Mapplethorpe exhibition (with more than just a behind).

Yet later in his youth, when Renee leaves his high school production early, he’s devastated. His mother Ellen (Jeanine Serralles) finally tells him the truth: Renee is an alcoholic. She always has been. What Joshua saw as eccentricity, Ellen has experienced as neglect and trauma. The idealized grandmother begins to fracture. The emotional core of We Had a World is the bond between grandson and grandmother, and how she’s shaped the artist he became. The central tension lies between the grandmother Joshua adores, and the mother Ellen endures.

The problem is in the execution. Tom, in The Glass Menagerie, concludes his opening by saying, “I think the rest of the play will explain itself.” We Had a World does the opposite. It over-narrates, rarely letting a moment stand on its own. Scenes are introduced, then layered with constant commentary. Whole stretches play as reenactments with footnotes, and no scene is allowed to run its full course. The three actors frequently slip into the voices of characters who aren’t present—imitating father, grandfather, cousin, a mimicry that flattens the emotional stakes. There’s no engine of desire or resistance pushing the story forward; there’s nothing like Amanda’s drive to find Laura a “gentleman caller.” Jeanine Serralles, as Ellen, often veers into overacting, perhaps to compensate for the lack of dramatic shape and structure. It all quickly grows tiresome; the story cannot simply sit. Can we not eavesdrop a little?

Still, the relationship between Joshua and Renee lends the play real warmth. Their bond is specific, textured, and affectionate. Joshua is compassionate and lovable, and Feldman leans into that, charting his growth from boy to man. Their final scenes are genuinely moving. Renee may have failed as a mother, but as a grandmother she tried—perhaps successfully.

But that relationship, as tender and well-acted as it is, isn’t enough to carry the play. The love behind Harmon’s memories is real. But without dramatic momentum, the play hovers above life instead of stepping inside it. We Had a World longs to capture the power and pain of the past, but resists the demands of the present—where theater lives. The result is emotionally earnest, but theatrically inert.

WE HAD A WORLD by Joshua Harmon; Directed by Trip Cullman.

With: Andrew Barth Feldman, Joanna Gleason, and Jeanine Serralles.

Sets by John Lee Beatty. Costumes by Kaye Voyce. Lights by Ben Stanton. Sound Design and Original Music by Sinan Rafik Zafar.

Now playing through May 11 at Manhattan Theatre Club, New York City Center Stage II, 131 W 55th St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 100 minutes, no intermission.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

It is 1964 in Harlem. 1964 was a year in which Martin Luther King’s sun was on the rise. This was the state of things when Alice Childress ripped the Band Aid off and wrote a “Wine In The Wilderness,” a play that deals with themes of mythic proportion.  The year before, 1963, witnessed the March On Washington for Jobs and Freedom.  250,000 people showed up and King’s “I have A Dream” speech entered the halls of history.  1964 brought the signing of the Civil Rights Act.  A few weeks after that signing, riots broke out in New York, Rochester and Philadelphia due to police violence and the chaos of rumors and facts.  The night in question takes place during those riots.  Bill  (Grantham Coleman) is holed up in his apartment making sketches of whatever.  It is what he does.  No matter bullets flying and police hollering outside.

Bill gets a call from his friend Sonny-man (Brooks Brantly) who has found, on  this crazy night, the perfect model for Bill’s triptych of Black Womanhood. Bill explains the project  to his friend Oldtimer (Milton Craig Nealy) who has just stopped in to hide some of the spoils he picked up out on the street – food, liquor new clothes)  The title of the triptych is “Wine In The Wilderness” from the Omar Khayyám poem.  The first is a painting of a child, “Black Girlhood,” the second is a picture of Abyssinian perfection in every way. The thirds has yet to be painted.  It will be of a lost woman, the product of what society does to black women.  She is as close to the bottom as you can get.  In one word, she is “nothing.”  And it is this woman that Sonny-man thinks he has found.
Soon Sonny-man shows up with his wife Cynthia (Lakisha Michelle May) and his trophy, Tommy (Olivia Washington).  A stranger in a strange land arrives out of the blue and turns a comfortable quartet of friends on its ear.
While the three in the know treat Tommy like a specimen, welcoming her but giving less than 100% of their time and energy, Tommy begins to gin up an agenda of her own.  As the walls begin to close in she pushes back, going so far as to use the “N” word with bravado, at one point saying she would rather be called one than treated like one.  It is only when she takes her place in the matter, dropping her wig and riot salvaged clothing for natural hair and a beautiful African wrap, that Bill sees her for the extraordinary creature she is.  Childress downs not let any of us off the hook with a satin ribbon.  No, no, she makes her characters work hard for a resolution that takes no prisoners.
This is play must have rocked folk’s socks off back in 1969.  The fact is, it is fresh and relevant today,  Just look around.
Two technic notes that feel off kilter – Mr. Colman cannot draw a lick.  How easy it would be to give him sketch pads with light drawings already on them so that he could trace away to his heart’s content.  The second odd element is Ms. Washington’s hair under the wig.  It is a stunning weave that provides an air of majesty to Tommy.  It is not,  however, what was being worn by black women in 1964.  The styling yanks us into 2025, and waters down the elements of specificity that the design team and director LaChanze have generated.  Just sayin’.
Wine in the Wilderness, by Alice Childress and directed by LaChanze.
Brooks Brantly, Grantham Coleman, Lakisha Michelle May, Milton Craig Nealy, Olivia Washington
Scenic Design Arnulfo Maldonado, Costume Design by Dede Ayite, Lighting Design Jeanette Oi-Suk Yew, Sound Design by Bill Toles, and Wig/Hair Design by Nikiya Mathis.
Through April 13 at Classic Stage Company, Manhattan; classicstage.org. Running time: 1 hour 25 minutes.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

By Tulis McCall

In “Purpose” the new play by Brandon Jacobs-Jenkins, everything happened because Nazareth “Naz” Jasper (Jon Michael Hill) and Aziza Houston (Kara Young) overslept, in separate beds, after she had driven hours to get to Niagara Falls and have Naz artificially inseminate her – Sonoma Turkey Baster if you please.  After the EVENT they stayed up talking as friends are wont to do and watching TV that was mainly white people killing each other as they are also wont to do.  Because they overslept, Aziza offered to drive Naz from Niagara Falls to a family celebration in Chicago.  The celebration is to honor Junior Jasper’s (Glenn Davis) release from prison where he was serving time for tax evasion (I think).  When the two arrive at the mansion, it is clear that there is a storm brewing, literal and figurative.  The two family heads Solomon “Sonny” Jasper (Harry Lennix) and his wife Claudine (Latanya Richardson Jackson) insist that Aziza stay overnight both because of the storm and because she is the first woman that Naz has ever brought home.  No pressure.

Are you with me?  No worries.   “Purpose” is a sprawling tale that collects plot points like a dark cashmere coat collects lint.  In the first act Naz is our narrator guiding us through some simple and predictable moves with grace.  He is charming and as surprised as we are then the you-know-what hits the fan.  The reason for the implosion and explosion is simple – Momma wants the family reputation to remain pristine.  Poppa was a leader in the church during the Civil Rights Movement.  Martin Luther King, whose portrait dominates the stage, was a close companion.  What is less known to the world out there was that Poppa had other close companions that may have resulted in a few more children to add to the family tree.

As for the brothers – Junior is mentally unstable and in an unhappy marriage to Morgan (Alana Arenas) who is waiting her turn for undeserved jail time.  Naz insists he is asexual.  Neither of these situations appeals to the family’s seniors, but the sons are not able or willing to tow the prescribed line.

What lights the family fuse, however, is that both seniors want to know the exact nature of Naz and Aziza’s relationship.  E-x-a-c-t.  We never get the lowdown on why this is the day of days and attention must be paid.   That lack of information is one of the many missing pieces that stay missing.

The first act is on the light side – with sitcom laughs coming regularly, many of which are created when Naz confides in us as if we were his only allies.  Well, maybe we are.

The second act is weighed down by Naz’s narration, and in fact we could do without it entirely.  The actions speak for themselves and no translation is needed.  For whatever reason, however, Jacobs-Jenkins does not trust that less is more.  Family squabble points are made, explained, and made again until we are bleary.  As well, if the narration were cut back or eliminated, the running time of this play would be reduced.  As it is, “Purpose” clocks in at a little over 2 hours and 45 minutes.  A flat 2 hours would be plenty.  Phylicia Rashad‘s direction often feels unconnected to the action, especially the dinner table scene during which we cannot see some of the family until they stand, and often cannot hear.   With a family as crazy as this one, some inventive staging combined with character specificity and attention to detail would have been welcome.

What saves this production is the actors – specifically Hill, Young and Arenas who give nuanced performances that splash this crazy family with needed light and color.  In many ways these tree ARE the outsiders.   The elders do not fare as well, and this is partially due to the text that has them boxed in, just as they are boxed in by their lives.

During the last monologue Naz gives us the final-final on everyone’s disposition.  It is only in those brief moments that he steps away from being a narrator and enters that heart space in which he reveals who he is and what is on his mind and who he truly is.  He breaks our hearts with just a few words.  Would that we had heard them earlier.  Jacobs-Jenkins has pulled back the curtain on more than just one family.  The finger points to all of us – what is public and what is private and how we navigate the paths we choose.

PURPOSE – By Branden Jacobs-Jenkins, Directed by Phylicia Rashad

WITH Latanya Richardson Jackson, Harry Lennix, Jon Michael Hill, Glenn Davis, Alana Arenas,  Kara Young

scenic design by Todd Rosenthal, costume design by Dede M. Ayite, lighting design by Amith Chandrashaker, and sound design by Rob Milburn and Michael Bodeen.

Through July 6 at the Helen Hayes Theater, Manhattan; purposeonbroadway.com. Running time: 2 hours 50 minutes.

I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

David Mills is nothing if not charming.  His is an eclectic presentation that depends on the weather, the current state of affairs (dismal and frightening) and who shows up to be entertained and entertaining.  On the night Mills was performing at Pangea in the East Village one of the audience members was from Ireland and had brought her mother.  Mills himself is a world citizen, having floated back and forth between London and New York for quite awhile, and much sweet attention was made to mother and daughter.

One gets the feeling that Mills dishes up what is currently on his mind, no matter if you understand or approve.  He is a pied piper on an adventure, and you are welcome to keep up.  His opening song “Am I Black  Enough For You” by Billy Paul is a perfect example because Mills is whiter than all of Finland.  Nevertheless he delivers the goods along with a brief explanation of who Billy Paul was (performed the hit single “Me and Mrs. Jones” in 1972 that was written by Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff, and  Cary Gilbert,.)  before moving along.

Rapid fire is Mills preferred tempo, but not so rapid that we fall out of step.  It appears to be his natural gait and when mellowed becomes one of Mills’ strongest assets.  He is at heart a storyteller (an overused term these days) or perhaps “raconteur” would be a better word.  He explains the difference between stand up and cabaret – cabaret has room for art.  Stand-up not so much.  After a moment of confessing that we are all interlopers, we move through several chapters meanderings where he discovers the Irish woman in the crowd who on whom he spends a good amount of time, recommending all the tourist attractions the rest of us avoid.

His first bout of raconteuring arrives disguised as an audio tour of the streets of Chelsea – complete with homeless, immigrants selling candy, people lying in the street, perches perfect for leaping, and in general civilization collapsing in on itself.  Each image is clear and handled with care.  “New York City has a way of resolving itself,“ he tells us.

Underneath it all is a mutual contempt we all share for one another – illustrated by “You Can’t Win,” from “The Wiz” – (Charlie Smalls.  His riff on Dune Two is a study in how to pull the gold out of a boring piece of entertainment.

His next audio journey wanders down the road of a lonely gay man in 1969 on a Caribbean island, man with a complicated past while he waits to be brought, “Something Cool.”  This is a jewel that lands with a gentle thud.

A brief spate of comments on drugs, where Mills wanders through a variety of subject as if we were all at an open air market.  This left half the room laughing so hard they were gasping for air.  Gay apps and swiping.  Being Old School in the day of apps and wishing they would bring back graffiti in the bathrooms.

Photo by Tim Redfern

Jody Shelton, Mills music director, is a perfect partner for all the shenanigans.  He laughs at all the jokes and knows exactly when and how to maneuver his way into the narration.  His timing is exquisite.

More talk about sex and loneliness and what danger lies in a stranger’s bedroom.  Mills tales are straightforward and take no prisoners as he puts a new twist on “Native New Yorker” (Odessa) and tosses off the comment that some days there can be too much laughter.

His final tale takes us to a bar in Fayetteville where obsession, sexual lines and identity blur.

Choctaw Bingo )Larry McMurtry) or as Mills calls it “Our New National Anthem” is an unsettling tune that Mills uses to leads us to the exit.

“If you want a new friend, elevate an acquaintance,” his mother told him.  As you leave you get the impression that this is exactly what Mills has been doing all night.

A delight.

 

David Mills at Pangea March 14.

title.rendered: The Great Privation (How to flip ten cents into a dollar)

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

In Soho Rep’s inaugural production at its temporary home at Playwrights Horizons, Nia Akilah Robinson gives us “The Great Privation (How to flip ten cents into a dollar).” Mrs. Freeman (Crystal Lucas-Perry) and her daughter, 16-year-old Charity (Clarissa Vickerie) appear as women connected to a graveyard in Philadelphia.  Their presence spans centuries, beginning with 1832 and ending with the present.  This is an intriguing premise that, if nothing else, will make you sit up and pay attention.  In 1832 Mrs. Freeman  and her daughter Charity are keeping vigil at the graveside of Moses Freeman, recently departed due to cholera.  Moses needs time to make the spiritual journey to Senegal where he will meet his ancestors.  Three days is the estimated time.  His body must not be disturbed for three days.

This, however, flies in the face of the body snatchers who routinely rob graves for medical research.  There is no mention of whether they also steal white bodies.  While the women keep vigil we are treated to a dose of African American history and POV’s.  Society is rigged, and Freeman has known that since she was on the receiving end of being double-crossed by Quakers when she was a girl.  She became a business woman and has passed on her experience and wisdom as best she can to her daughter.

In the present day Missy (Lukas-Perry) and Charity are counselors at a children’s camp run by a church that is adjacent to the same graveyard.  Their co-worker John (Miles G. Jackson) is an openly gay Philly native with secrets weighing him down.  The head of camp operations, Cuffee (Holiday) is a mediocre leader at best who is struggling with his own sexual identity while fumbling with his administrative duties.

Robinson’s intention is to interlace these two sets of women, literally and figuratively.  It is a fascinating conceit that is hindered by the exposition layered throughout the story.  There is little action to keep the play moving forward which is disappointing because the premise is so rich.  There is also a digital clock handing above the set that never connects to the story.  (Remember the clock on the building south of Union Square – it is like that).  And finally there is the title of the play.  I am guessing “The Great Privation” is a play on “The Great Migration” but the slug line is a mystery.

Evren Odcikin‘s  direction is so light it is hardly visible.  Blocking is awkward.  Actors give uneven performances  with Lucas-Perry maintaining a steady pace, Vickerie leaping from zero to sixty several time with no explanation and Jackson achieving lift-off as the lost but well intentionem repressed gay counselor.  Holiday gets few chances to shine but makes the most of his moments.

As I said – this play will make you think.  It is chock-a-block full of history that should be common knowledge but is not.    Next time out Robinson could use a plot that lives up to the tale she has to tell.  I hope there will be more forthcoming.    And PS the temporary home of Soho Rep at Playwrights seems to be working out very well.

The Great Privation (How to flip ten cents into a dollar), by Nia Akilah Robinson,  directed by Evren Odcikin

WITH Crystal Lucas-Perry, Holiday, Miles G. Jackson and Clarissa Vickerie

The creative team includes scenic designer Mariana Sanchez, costume designer Kara Harmon, lighting designer Marika Kent, sound designer Tosin Olufolabi, video designer and programmer Maxwell Bowman, wig and hair designer Cookie Jordan, props supervisor Jackson Berkley, dramaturgy consultant Arminda Thomas, sensitivity specialist Ann C. James, voice and dialect coach Xavier Clark.

Through March 26.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Above Ground – Not Exactly a Comedy

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Currently playing at The Club at La Mama is a meaningful assembly of ten actors who have been working together for five years with a technique called real-time acting (stemming from Brecht and the Open Theater) developed by Paul Binnerts and Nancy Gabor. The group is called You’re Never Too Old to Play and their ages range from 74 to 98. The show they’re presenting is called Above Ground – Not Exactly a Comedy.

It’s a personal show of monologues and a couple of group exercises that touch on what its like to still be ticking after treading on this coil for numerous decades. They address hopes and dreams, both realized and not, death, illness, art, and childhood memories that shaped who they are. The vignettes were developed through improvisation, dance, and are framed by music.

One of the things that struck me with the presentation was the time that was taken, time to breath, time to be, and time to listen. The actors weren’t in any hurry to go anywhere, and so why should we be. That connection with the audience was as much the show (and the technique) as the stories they told. It was refreshing in this hurried pace of a world we live in that often seems just the opposite, to sit and just be, to acknowledge the actors and the audience and where we all were at that moment.

I also came away from the evening feeling that I had participated somewhat in their lives, shared who they were and got to live by and with them for a little while. It was a nice feeling.

Using music and filmed mirror images of the actors and their movements, the show did not slow down or falter in its progression as it  played with, “the reality of the illusion (that is live theater), not the illusion of the reality.”

The best way to describe the feeling I walked away with, was lovely. It was a lovely evening.

Remember, you’re never too old to play

—–

Above Ground -Not Exactly a Comedy was directed by Nancy Gabor and Paul Binnerts.

The actors are Ilana Abramovitch, Susan Binet, Nora Galer, Jonathan Ned Katz, Christine Koenig, Gloria Miguel, Sally Plass, Joanne Riel, Lorraine Marx-Singer, and Harold Thomas.

Soundtrack is by Paul Binnarts.

March 13 to 23, 2025

Presented by La MaMa E.T.C. (The Club), 74A East Fourth Street

Thursdays through Saturdays at 7:30 PM, Sundays at 3:00 PM

Adults: $30, Students/Seniors: $25. First ten tickets are $10 (limit 2 per person).

Buy tickets: <www.lamama.org> and <https://web.ovationtix.com/trs/pr/1227052>, (646) 430-5374.

Running time: 60 min.

title.rendered: I Can’t Believe It’s Not Ireland!

content.rendered:
By David Walters

The talented Paddy Cullivan (comedian, educator, showman, satirist, composer, and musician) is traveling the States with his one-man “historical entertainment,” I Can’t Believe It’s Not Ireland! There’s only one show left in his US tour, March 14 at Port Jefferson, Long Island. If you are in the area, and are interested in hearing about the past, present, and future of Ireland from a man with both radical and sane views, this is an entertainment that will educate you, make you laugh, force you to think differently, and come away with a positive attitude about what the world can be. This is a show about the possible future, but the only way to get there is through the past.

Utilizing a slide show presentation format and AI art, Paddy takes his audience through the long history of what brought Ireland to where it is today, taking his way-back machine to the beginnings with the early migrations from the long-lost cousins the Ukrainians. He then goes through the disparate tribes and their falling ins and outs, goes through the kings, their alliances and betrayals, and stops long and hard to take a look at Theobald Wolfe Tone. Wolfe is considered by Mr. Cullivan to be ground zero for Ireland’s unification. His writings put forth that Ireland could not truly move forward as a country unless it became one.

An enlightening portion of the show followed a cab driver from Northern Ireland, who had never been to the South, on his first trip there. He is struck over and over again about how English it is. So English that it frightens him, and he must scurry back up North. The cabbies’ observations on Dublin and its environs are both funny and strikingly true.

“It’s not where you’re from, it’s where you’re going,” is the theme of the evening as Paddy rounds out his presentation with ways that Ireland can move forward, and in essence rule the world. Controversial, yes (no longer call it Ireland, but Hibernia instead), but also pragmatic in the approach. One of the striking ideas he put forth to further go down the road of a united Ireland, is to eliminate the tri-color flag. His belief, and I went away feeling the same, is that every time someone looks at it, they can’t help but continue the partition of Ireland. The green and the orange are permanently apart on that flag, never to meet, never to come together. They are separated by a peaceful field of white, but there is no possible way they could touch. (He also mentioned that the two colors look awful together, “Would you paint your house those colors?” Point well made.) Paddy uses historical references (he shows a world map with multiple examples) to back up his claim that partition never works out well, anywhere it’s been enforced.

If you are near Port Jefferson on March 14th and are interested in Ireland, do take the opportunity to give a listen to Mr. Cullivan’s ideas, comedy, and music. You’ll walk away better for it. Tickets can be had HERE.

———-

When I saw it Paddy’s show was performed at The New York Irish Center (NYIC), 1040 Jackson Avenue in Long Island City. Now in its 20th year, NYIC is a, “hub for culture and community presenting and produces more than 100 cultural and community events a year, serving a rapidly evolving Irish diaspora, and eagerly welcoming other cultural communities to join and collaborate.” They are a true community organization with many programs that touch everyone.  They are currently running a series of multi-cultural music jams that look fascinating.

Paddy Cullivan’s US Tour I Can’t Believe It’s Not Ireland

Mar 14 – Port Jefferson, NY

title.rendered: Judy Collins and Friends: 85 Years of Music and Protest at The Town Hall

content.rendered:
by Betsyann Faiella

The incredible and timeless Judy Collins celebrated her 85th birthday at The Town Hall on Saturday, March 8th with a group of pals and colleagues that spanned the six decades of her career. Since I don’t think it’s fair to review what was essentially a tribute and a party, I’ll just comment that it was a gorgeous lovefest for a supremely talented and generous performer, even if everything didn’t go exactly as planned (late in the evening).

Collins opened (in one of several gorgeous ensembles she wore during the nearly three-hour show) with songs from her resplendent and varied repertoire: “Mountain Girl” (Judy Collins and Jonas Fjeld), “Masters of War” (Bob Dylan and Jean Ritchie), “John Riley” (a traditional English folk song) and “Both Sides Now” (Joni Mitchell).

Collins gave a start to many composers who were just beginning to show themselves, so her repertoire is full of music from others, as well as her own compositions. The audience was treated to her social commentary songs and her timeless folk-rock songs and ballads.

Her soaring high notes and beautiful storytelling and phrasing were truly awe-inspiring, and, in fact, Rickie Lee Jones mentioned, shaking her head in disbelief, Collins’ phenomenal ability to reach and sustain high notes at the age of 85.

Along with the guests who showed up in the flesh, there were remembrances of many others including Bob Dylan and Leonard Cohen, whose song “Suzanne” was recorded by Collins for her album, In My Life, in 1966. She told the story of meeting the late Cohen, at the time a novelist and nerdy poet who lacked confidence and said he wasn’t sure he was a songwriter, then played her “Suzanne.” The rest is history, as they say.

The prolific Collins is well known for her stories and saucy humor and she did not disappoint, surprising her duet and recent writing partner Ari Hest by revealing she’d had an affair with someone he’d just mentioned, just as matter of fact as if she’d said, “he was such a nice guy. ”

Collins, who was a student of classical piano from a very young age, took to the keys and performed “The Blizzard,” an absorbing story song about a stranger, a Colorado night and getting stuck in a storm. It was her only time at the piano during the evening, leaving that up to Russell Walden, except for the moment when Stephen Schwartz came on stage to accompany – and duet with her –  on “Over The Rainbow” (Harold Arlen and Yip Harburg). You make a lot of fabulous and varied friends through the years when you’re brilliant.

Justin Vivian Bond performed a compelling version of “Marat Sade,” (Judy Collins) and was followed by the extraordinary Martha Redbone singing “Dreamers”  (Judy Collins), acapella.

Paula Cole magically reinvented “My Father” (Judy Collins)  – as if it could be any more beautiful!

Two old pals of Collins made their way to the stage towards the end of the evening: Richard Thompson and then, in a suit and tie,  Stephen Stills, the romantic partner in the aforementioned affair! Apparently, it was a short dalliance, but impactful enough for him to have written “Suite: Judy Blue Eyes” in her honor. Stills mentioned directly to Collins that although she broke his heart, he knew she “had married the right guy.” He said, “Man, Louis was great.” Collins, taken aback, explained she had just lost her husband and companion of 46 years, the industrial designer Louis Nelson, on Dec. 3rd. She was so obviously touched by Stills’ comment, that she hugged him warmly, and thanked him.

Judy Collins is a splendid woman inside and out, and her talent and influence on songwriting is a legacy that has grown over six 6 decades  and a discography that consists of 36 studio albums, nine live albums, numerous compilation albums, four holiday albums, and 21 singles (at least!).

The whole evening was pretty much delicious. A triumph.

Additional performers and guests: Oakland Rain, Sophie B. Hawkins. Writer/journalist Molly Jong-Fast.

Music Directors: Russ Titelman and Russell Walden.

Band: Thad DeBrock, Zev Katz, Doug Yowell

Sound: Sean Loughry

Producer: Katherine DePaul

Publicity: Keith Sherman & Associates

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Taming of the Shrew, Frog & Peach Theatre Co’s latest production, presents one of Shakespeare’s most controversial work: a cast of characters inhabiting a world where  financial power outweighs personal integrity and women are meant to be tame, specifically tamed wives. Cullum Theater at American Theatre of Actors is the perfect setup for this Shakespearean production, under the direction of Lynnea Benson. The stage fills with women walking a sort of runway, flaunting their  legs, bodices, and lace attire. Robes are pulled open, hips thrusting forward, little dance moves center-stage. The men look on in disdain, embarrassment, complete and utter disapproval and confusion. These are not tame women! 

Bianca (Camelia Iturregui Fuertes) and Katarina (Amy Frances Quint), the two daughters of Baptista (Vivien Landau) are to be married. And of course, dowries are crucial in this decision to choose the most suitable husband. But, there’s a catch: Baptista wants to find a husband for her eldest daughter, Katarina, before obedient Bianca can wed. Who will undertake the woo-ing of Cursed Katarine? Who can “woo the wildcat,” the one with the “scolding tongue?” Both young and very old suitors disguised as tutors come to woo Bianca, while Baptista laughs at Petruchio’s (DazMann Still) confidence in woo-ing her daughter.

Frog & Peach Theatre Co‘s press release says that the production “delivers a fast-paced beautifully acted performance that remains true to the Bard’s text while resonating with modern audiences.” This cast translates each line into action in a way that I care more about how the characters interact with each other than I do the theme of taming women and deceiving their families in hopes of gaining financial fortune.

Despite this piece being known for its mysoginism and manipulation of women, I found this production humorous and enjoyable–not annoyingly mysoginistic like it most certainly could have been!

DazMann Still (Petruchio) immediately stands out as contender for Katarina’s (Kate) heart. While Petruchio and his flamboyant outfit marries Kate against her will (although I expected more of a fight and was somewhat rooting for them, anyways) he tries to “tame” her by getting into disagreements and petty arguments, talk to her incessantly while she’s trying to sleep, and starve her. Imagine how much quicker she could have grown to like him without all of her discomfort?! But–all of this was done with the intention of “kindness;” he wanted to somehow kill her with faux kindness.

Grumio (James Nash) is equally engaging to watch: Petruchio’s personal assistant who sits at the edge of the stage picking at threads and stones and down his pants, and his feet. I couldn’t stop staring at him massaging his own feet. Everything unacceptable for public behavior, he does. And I am totally enthralled by each of these charcater’s intricacies. Each individual in this performance has defined, distinguished characters.  The direction for this play made the men and women balanced in some way, a way the Bard’s script alone does not. Intelligence of women vs. the keen deceit of men. Both fall short in some ways, as is the human way, but both sexes are spitfires with confidence.

While I am not a frequent attender of Shakespearean shows–I did thoroughly enjoy this evening in the audience of Taming of the Shrew. While I lost track the several men (and all their “i-“ending names), I understood that Bianca had already chosen a suitor (Anuj Parikh) from the bunch, but men continue to prowl when a fortune is on the table. And as the Bard does, there was of course an even higher deceit through a suitor framing himself and his “father” as a father and son that did in fact havea fortune.

I may not be a Shakespeare aficionado, but this company’s performance and passion completely engaged me.

Directed by Lynnea Benson, Co-Founder and Artistic Director of Frog & Peach Theatre Co.

CAST: Amy Frances Quint (Katarina), Anuj Parikh (Lucentio), Camelia Iturregui Fuertes (Bianca), DazMann Still (Petruchio), David Elyha (Signore Gremio), Ellen Lanese (Donatella, u/s Baptista), Eric Swanson (Tranio), Fernando Gamarra (Gianni, a constable, u/s Vincentio), Hari Bhaskar (Biondello), Jaixa Irizarry (Widow), James Nash (Grumio), John L. Payne (Vincentio), Kenneth Michael (Curtis, u/s Biondello), Kezia Tyson (u/s Kate, Ensemble), Lenny Ciotti (Hortensio), Mark Vaughn (Antonio, a constable, u/s Gremio), Nina David (a courtesan of Padua, Sugarsop, u/s Widow), Padraig Bond (Tailor, Fight Captain, u/s Hortensio & Grumio), Steven Ungar (The Pendant), Venkatesh Vohra (Haberdasher, Ensemble, u/s Lucentio & Tranio), Vivien Landau (Baptista).

CREATIVE TEAM: Asa Benally (Costume Designer), Tierney Brennan (Set Design), JJ Jayaraman (Lighting Design), Marcus Watson (Violence Coordinator), Mathew Seepersad (Stage Manager).

Taming of the Shrew plays at Cullum Theater at American Theatre of Actors, 314 W 54th St, New York, NY 10019. Running time is 1hr, 45 minutes with one intermission. Performances run Thursday, Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays until March 23, 2025.

Tickets start at $34.95 and are available for purchase here.

Students with valid school ID can purchase tickets for just $24.99 for performances thru 3/16/25.  For Theatre Lovers ages 65+, just $24.99 through 3/16/25. Prices are slightly higher at the door.

Educators: Group rates may be available for school classes. Please contact frogandpeachtheatreco@gmail.com for more information.

excerpt.rendered: Bianca and Katarina, the two daughters of Baptista (Vivien Landau) are to be married. And of course, dowries are crucial in this decision to choose the most suitable husband. But, there’s a catch: Baptista wants to find a husband for her eldest daughter, Katarina, before obedient Bianca can wed. Who will undertake the woo-ing of Cursed Katarine? Who can “woo the wildcat,” the one with the “scolding tongue?”This cast translates each line into action in a way that I care more about how the characters interact with each other than I do the theme of taming women and deceiving their families in hopes of gaining financial fortune.
