content.rendered:
The Jonathan Larson Project, presented at the Orpheum Theatre and conceived by Jennifer Ashley Tepper, is a loving scrapbook of a mythic figure whose legacy extended far beyond his tragically short time with us. Longtime fans and the uninitiated alike can find something to love from this fantastically realized vision of Jonathan Larson’s work. If you, like me, spent your adolescence competing with fellow theatre kids to see who could remember the right words to “La Vie Boheme” or if you, also like me, grew into the kind of adult who finds “30/90” a little too real, The Jonathan Larson Project is for you. If this is your first time diving into Larson’s musical vision, it is an immersive introduction to a talent whose work changed the face of Broadway and elevated causes like the queer rights and environmental advocacy long before they were in the mainstream.

The songs presented here are by no means perfect, and even I cringed at some of the lyrics. But the show makes it clear that what we are hearing is intentionally undisturbed archival material. These are the drafts of songs left behind by a man who did not know it would be the last time he could edit them, as Larson famously passed away at the age of 35 on the night that his hit musical RENT premiered. Sitting in the East Village theatre and listening to people talk about the ways that Larson changed their life felt like gathering with old friends to have a drink and remember a loved one.

Lauren Marcus, Andy Mientus, Jason Tam, Taylor Iman Jones, Adam Chanler-Berat. Photo by Joan Marcus.

The show seems to be plucked right from Larson’s endearingly neurotic mind. This isn’t just a tribute; it’s a natural extension of the universe he created. The stage evokes the DIY spirit of RENT with exposed lights, a fire escape ladder, and interspersed TVs that are reminiscent of Maureen’s protest performance. The costumes and big personalities of each cast member reflect the merry band of artists and eccentrics who populate both RENT and Tick, Tick… BOOM! For a certain kind of theatregoer, finding out that there is a way to extend our time in the worlds that Larson created is a true blessing. That joy is reflected in the exuberant performances of songs like “Greene Street,” a full cast number that had not previously been performed or recorded, and was written during Larson’s first year in New York.

The cast is well-rounded, showcasing a variety of acting and singing styles that are perfectly suited for the blend of pop and musical numbers. Lauren Marcus’ manic energy and bright tone animate numbers like “Hosing the Furniture,” a song that imagines the stress of a housewife in the future and was written by Larson to impress his mentor, Stephen Sondheim. Taylor Iman Jones shines bright in every number, gripping the audience from the first, sultry note of Larson’s pop song “Out of My Dreams.” She deserved every long applause break that she got. Adam Chanler-Berat, Jason Tam, and Andy Mientus are Larson male protagonists personified, with voices that sail through high notes and rock-inspired ballads.

Taylor Iman Jones and Andy Mientus. Photo by Joan Marcus.

The flow of songs is also well-curated, moving from emotional numbers that plumb the depths of the characters’ psyches to fiery, protest songs that seem to predict the current moment, including “The Truth is a Lie” and “The Vision Thing,” which lampoon corrupt politicians who are more interested in optics than helping the people they claim to serve. Sound familiar?

What the songs lack in polish, the show makes up for using the collaborative strength of a creative team who were determined to do justice to their muse. If you have any love for Jonathan Larson, or you want to explore a part of theatre and NYC history that has pressing implications for the current moment, this is the show to see.

THE JONATHAN LARSON PROJECT – Conceived by Jennifer Ashley Tepper; Directed by John Simpkins

WITH: Adam Chanler-Berat, Taylor Iman Jones, Lauren Marcus, Andy Mientus, Jason Tam

At the Orpheum Theater, (212) 477-2477. Through June 1. Running time: 90 minutes.

For more information and tickets, please visit www.thejonathanlarsonproject.com.

By Yuval Jonas

The Mint Theater Company finds overlooked plays from the past and brings them to life; they’ve proved their prowess with this staging of Harold Brighouse’s 1915 Garside’s Career. Brighouse is best known for Hobson’s Choice, which was adapted into a film in 1954 by David Lean. This production of a lesser-known work takes us to early 20th century England and shows why the company’s mission matters.

Peter Garside, played with conviction and energy by Daniel Marconi, is a working-class man who’s been accepted into university—a rare achievement for his background. His mother, portrayed with sharp comedic timing by Amelia White, proudly declares that this news will “spread fast, like murder.”

Garside loves public speaking. His fiancée Margaret (Madeline Seidman) warns him of its dangers, telling him that “the itch to speak ruins people” and “is like the itch to drink—only cheaper.” But his oratorical talent is undeniable, and the Labour Party encourages him to run for Parliament. Though Margaret urges him to stay on a more stable path, ambition wins out, and Garside quickly ascends from humble beginnings to political prominence.

The production captures his transformation. We move from his mother’s modest home to his lavish new London residence (he brings his mother with him.) Kindall Almond’s costumes morph to reflect their climb up the social ladder. As success consumes Garside, he abandons both Margaret and his principles for a new romantic interest, the aristocratic Gladys Mottram (Sara Haider), and the trappings of high society. One memorable scene blends drawing-room romance with political intrigue: as an angry crowd gathers outside, Garside tells Mottram that he can master a mob any night, but the chance to be with her is a rare opportunity. The story recalls Robert Penn Warren’s novel All the King’s Men: both follow a man whose gift for speech propels him to power, only for ambition, money, and influence to corrode his ideals.

When his constituents discover that he has betrayed the working class, they come to confront him in London. “I’ve fallen like Lucifer fell, never to rise again,” he laments. The story has the bones of a Greek tragedy—Garside is warned about the dangers of ambition but charges ahead anyway—and is infused with the wit and social critique of Coward and Shaw.

By the final act, Garside and his mother have returned to their provincial town and modest life. Disgraced, he fears being a “has been,” but Margaret, who has always understood him best, returns to rescue him from despondency. “Now we’re a little bit less in love with life, but we’re still here, the both of us,” she tells him. She pleads with him to abandon public life and become a mechanic. When he frets that his genius will go to waste, her response is simple: “You are genius enough for me.” The most important thing was in front of him all along—an honest and loving relationship.

Brighouse’s play and this production deliver the good old enjoyment of theater—a compelling story, told by a talented ensemble under effective direction, that draws us into another world.

I was previously unfamiliar with the Mint Theater Company. Now, I’ll be looking forward to what comes next.

GARSIDE’S CAREER by Harold Brighouse; Directed by Matt Dickson.

With: Erik Gratton, Sara Haider, Daniel Marconi, Melissa Maxwell, Paul Niebanck, Michael Shantz, Madeline Seidman, Amelia White, and Avery Whitted.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

Sumo wrestling is the official sport of Japan.  Dating back to before the first century, Sumo has gone in and out of popularity since its beginning.  From an agricultural ritual, to a deadly battle, to a military training regimen, to a sponsored sport and a spiritual practice, Lisa Sanaye Dring explores Sumo’s place in the modern world by looking at six rikishi (wrestlers) studying and vying for the top ranking of Ozeki.

Dring’s exploration in SUMO, playing at the Public Theater through the end of the month, is both reverent of the sport’s history and paying homage to its spirituality, while infusing a modern narrative and perspective; looking at the sport through the lens of very modern characters. She honors tradition with serious movement, but in act two infuses joy and individuality by incorporating elements of the movement practice into a karaoke dance sequence.  Throughout the piece, actors don a serious and respectful tone, although the tension is sometimes diffused in moments of escaped modern quips and phrases.  Through this dichotomy, Dring explores the traditions and rituals that define us while examining and stripping away those that harm us.

David Shih and Scott Keiji Takeda in SUMO; photo by Joan Marcus

In SUMO, we follow Aiko (Scott Keiji Takeda), a new and eager rikishi who has entered this heya (stable) to learn how to be a sumo wrestler.  Entering in the lowest rank of Maezumō, Aiko must sweep and clean the heya, cook and serve meals for the other wrestlers, and bathe and wait on the resident Ozeki, Mistsou (David Shih).  We follow Aiko’s journey as he gets to know the other wrestlers and understands their relationship to themselves, sumo, and each other.

The first act of the show ends with an exciting and energy-infused honbasho (sumo match).  We – like Aiko, finally ready to fight after his training – are finally ready to watch, having sat with the ritual and earned the right to appreciate this sacred sport.  The wrestling, which continues heavily into the second act, is a beautiful battle of the bodies. Through James Yaegashi and Chelsea Pace’s choreography and direction, the sumo dance reads as an exciting sports match, the audience is invested in their athlete and can’t look away.

The ensemble cast shine in SUMO, bringing beauty and strength to not only the art form but their characters as well, and infusing life into Dring’s search for clarity and meaning within ritual and tradition.  Ren, played by Ahmad Kamal, brings a particular warmth to the stage, serving as Aiko’s mentor in not only sumo wrestling, but also in building community and finding strength in love while using one’s body to fight in the ring.

Set designer Wilson Chin builds out the heya (stable) on the stage, with a dohyō at center, through which actors wrestle physically and emotionally with each other and themselves in Raph B. Peña’s expertly crafted movement.  Projections by Hana S. Kim remind us of the spiritual practice of sumo, which began as a fight between two gods and is embodied as a woman spirit who is seen by only those who have truly discovered the soul of the sport.

While SUMO is a piece about wrestling and tradition, the play encompasses so much more about humanity, spirituality, and sacrifice.  Sumo, as a sport, is mired in honor and strength, and Dring’s play dares to ask us where our true strengths lie and what we value most: winning or community?  Can there be space for both strength and compassion?  I would argue that Dring is telling us that winning the battle against yourself, that in finding community and losing ego, that that is where she (Sumo) truly lives.

 

SUMO – by Lisa Sanaye Dring; directed by Ralph B. Peña

FEATURING: Kris Bona, Red Concepción, Akira Fukui, Michael Hisamoto, Ahmad Kamal, Earl T. Kim, Hank Lin, Haowen Luo, David Shih, Scott Keiji Takeda, Paco Tolson, and Viet Vo.

Scenic design by Wilson Chin; costumes by Mariko Ohigashi; lighting by Paul Whitaker; sound and music composition by Fabian Obispo; hair, wig and makeup design by Alberto “Albee” Alvarado; projection design by Hana S. Kim; prop design by Thomas Jenkeleit; taiko drum composition and performance by Shih-Wei Wu; sumo consultant and co-fight direction by James Yaegashi; co-fight direction and intimacy direction by Chelsea Pace.  Produced by: Ma-Yi  Theater company (Raph B. Peña, producing artistic director) and The Public Theater (Oskar Eustis, artistic director; Patrick Willingham, executive director).  At the Public Theater (425 Lafayette Street). https://publictheater.org/productions/season/2425/sumo/

title.rendered: Urban Stages Dynamic Duo one-act winners – The Audit and The American Dream

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Two plays, one powerful connection.

After 300 submissions, culling that list, and a round of readings of eight semi-finalists, two winning plays from Urban Stages’ Dynamic Duos competition (two-character one-acts on any subject), have been paired and given a production. The Audit, by Lynda Crawford, and The American Dream, by Juan Ramirez Jr., currently running together on the same bill through March 16.

What’s surprising is that with no restriction on subject matter, the two winners both tackle the same theme, human connection.

In The Audit, Sam (Joel Ripka) is about to receive an IRS auditor in his small apartment to examine his claims of home office. Like his life, his finances are in complete disarray, his musical creativity, which is his work, has dried up, and his cat, on death’s door, needs an operation to survive. And there’s no money. Auditor Edie (Disnie Sebastien) arrives on the scene with the emotional shield of numbers and strict tax rules. What comes to light as Sam reveals his mess of a life is that Edie’s personal story is in just as much disarray as Sam’s and their “Life ain’t fair” connection develops as they discover that they have more in common than they first realized. They end up as two human beings hugging at the end, and the mark of a good play is that such a moment feels well-earned. It does.

The American Dream begins with the door opening to a barley-furnished room and Corina (Libe Barer) being roughly escorted into the space by Efron (Juan Ramirez, Jr.) and told to stand on a piece of cardboard on the floor. We become witnesses to the last leg of a journey north to the U.S. by a coyote (migrants pay coyotes a fee to guide them across the border) and his charge. Half the fee has been paid, but they have to wait in this room for the rest to be wired from her husband before Corina can be released. The signal that the money is in the account will come from a phone call. If the money is not deposited by a certain time, Corina will either be killed or forced to become a sex worker. What ensues is the building of pressure, Corina fighting with her wits for her life, and Efron hoping to not have to kill again as his past actions have come to haunt his psyche. This play is super relevant to today and the immediacy of the situation is palpable. Putting a character in a plausible life-and-death situation is not easy on the stage, but writer/actor Ramirez has accomplished this difficult task with a story that reaches across the footlights and into the audience.

The writing in both of these plays is very strong, relevant, and timely. The human connections they portray of mutual understanding are relatable and truthful as the characters all seek a better life.

—–

The Audit is written by Lynda Crawford and directed by Leigh Selting,

The American Dream is written by Juan Ramirez and directed by Maria Mileaf.

The design team for both shows: Benny Pitt – scenic design; Elena Vannoni – costume design; Sinjin Reinhard – lighting design; David Lawson – sound design; Kim Sharp – projection design; David Anzuelo – fight director; Jon Pierson – original music for The Audit.

Urban Stages Theater, 259 West 30th Street, in Manhattan, through March 16, 2025

For tickets, visit https://www.urbanstages.org/doublebill

Running time: two hours including one intermission

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

What kept running through my head as I watched New Group‘s  “Curse Of The Starving Class” at The Pershing Square Signature Center was: “This is a whackadoodle play.”  For the record, I don’t say that often.  Full disclosure – I am not very very very familiar with Sam Shepard’s work.  Or I have forgotten what little I knew.  I do remember seeing “True West” several times after it was filmed.  I did see “A Lie of the Mind” back in the 1980’s.

The only thing that all these plays bring to mind is that nobody was happy.  Nobody was happy and they were taking pleasure in making certain that they did their best to curtail any jocularity that might cross the threshold.  The only good news was bad news.

“Curse of the Starving Class” fits nicely into this pattern.  A woebegone family living in rural California has begun their slide into oblivion.  As the show opens we see nothing special on the very detailed set by Arnulfo Maldonado:  the usual kitchen detritus of blender, toaster, a table and a cooking island that takes up too much space.  When Wesley Tate (Cooper Hoffman) enters with a vacuum, dustpan and brush, we notice that the clear sliding glass doors are clear because there is no glass in them.  Ditto the windows above the kitchen sink.  As Wes sweeps up the mess, his mother Ella (a semi-catatonic Calista Flockhart) shuffles into the kitchen.  The next few minutes are spent as Ella revs up to arguing speed.  And there is a lot to argue about, beginning with the perpetrator of the broken everything, patriarch Weston Tate (Christian Slater) whose whereabouts are unknown and about whom no one cares.  May he rest in peace someplace other than home.  Neither Hoffman nor Flockhart seem to have a grip on the language or the situation at hand.  It is not until Emma Tate (Stella Marcus) enters that we experience someone who, in horse parlance, is up to the bit – paying attention, engaged and reacting.  While this makes us perk up, there is not much more to hang on to.  We are on a downward trajectory that will not be stopped.

The nut of the nut here is that both Ella and Weston have concluded that the only way out of this hole into which they have dug themselves is to sell the house, the land and the livestock (including one very alive sheep [Lois)].  Lois makes more than one appearance, steals every scene she is in, and can barely walk on the slippery linoleum. Not to mention she has to endure a lot of loud noise, including banging trash cans and plain old screaming.  The Humane Society should pop by for a look-see.

No surprise that the Tate duo are not successful at the attempted sale because that is their lot in life and will be forever more.  Their children fare no better.

The end.

The part that matters here is that we (meaning me) ended up not caring about any of these people.  No matter the monologues that they deliver in self defense.  These are verbal blips that don’t move the meter.  Why this choice for a play is a mystery (several audience members stood up and cheered so I am in the minority) and Scott Elliott’s direction seems casual at best.  A couple of odd moments: Hoffman must deliver his monologue sitting at the edge of the stage.  The audience is packed in so tight that he has to look over the heads of the people directly in front of him.  He does his best, but it is an awkward moment.  Ditto for him scrounging through the provision in the refrigerator – this he does with his back to us.

What does work is Christian Slater’s portrayal of a drunk Weston Tate.  Most actors will tell you that in order to play drunk one must play against it.  Avoid being sloppy.  Be precise.  Slater’s work is pristine.  I bet he scared the crap out of the cast when they first saw him perform.  He did me.  He also made me care about Weston Tate for a few moments.  That’s something.

Christian Slater and Lois; Photo by Monique Carboni

For the most part, however, I was neither interested nor concerned.   None of the characters were exceptional.  I don’t believe that was Shepard’s intention.  Better luck next time.

Curse Of The Starving Class by Sam Shepard, directed by Scott Elliott

WITH David Anzuelo, Kyle Beltran, Calista Flockhart, Cooper Hoffman, Jeb Kreager, Stella Marcus and Christian Slater

This production includes Scenic Design byArnulfo Maldonado, Costume Design by Catherine Zuber, Lighting Design by Jeff Croiter and Sound Design by Leah Gelpe.  Production Supervisor is Five Ohm.

Tickets HERE EXTENDED through April 6.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Kinan Azmeh and CityBand present Live in Berlin

content.rendered:
By Victoria Lynne Dammer

With the February 28 release of his 14th album Live in Berlin, clarinetist and composer Kinan Azmeh, accompanied by CityBand guitarists Kyle Sanna, John Meyers and drummer John Hadfield, graced the stage at the packed dinner theater at Joe’s Pub and brought with them the sorrowful yet ever strong soul of music from Azmeh’s home country of Syria and so much more.

Azmeh, born in war torn Damascus and Brooklyn based, is a world-renowned soloist and composer, having played with New York Philharmonic and as far away as the Syrian Symphony Orchestra. He has shared the stage with musical notables such as Yo-Yo Ma, Aynur and Jivan Gasparian, among others.

Azmeh opened the show with a clarinet solo, undertones of base, entitled The Queen Commanded, a weeping and heartfelt tempo accompanied by the softness of drums that rose to a sort of frenzy, then softly finished like the end of lovemaking. The first song transitioned into the melody, The Translator, mesmerizing the audience with the haunting beauty of the two compositions.

Azmeh said the music presents the melody and tragedy of millions of perished Syrians.

Azmeh added, the atrocities in Syria inspired the music, quickly adding, “The dictator is gone and the melody survived,” regarding the recent news Assad had fled the country. These words dispersed resounding applause.

The song Jizleen, dedicated to a small town near Damascus, a village Azmeh used to visit on weekends, blessed us with its beauty. They planted trees and worked the land with family, then the village was chemically attacked during the war and the trees bulldozed. The song pays homage to the town and trees.

The celestial tune “Galileo Galilee,” composed by guitarist Sanna, started off with a sad weeping, the soft timber of chimes and the slight touch on the edge of the cymbals. It worked its way to an increased tempo, an explosive inclusion of clarinet, and ended with an intense call to the heavens. The piece intertwined drums and guitars to the delight of all in attendance.

Perhaps the most inspiring piece of the night was Wedding. Azmeh said it represented the spirit in Syria of a village wedding and the number of drinks during the wedding increased the tempo.

Kinan Azmeh and CityBand will be touring in several U.S. cities and in Europe in the next few months. Try to attend their concert as they pay homage to a country that needs to rebuild their souls and soil.

Kinan Azmeh and CityBand, featuring guitarists Kyle Sanna, John Meyers and drummer John Hadfield, present their album release Live in Berlin at Joe’s Pub, 425 Lafayette Street, NYC. Press by amt public relations.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Conversations with Mother is a simple sitcom. This new semi-autobiographical comedy, written by Matthew Lombardo, and playing at New York City’s Theater 555, is about a gay man’s (Matt Doyle) childhood, turbulent jobs and relationships, and struggles and triumphs on his journey as a struggling addict and playwright–his mother (Caroline Aaron) is constant, supportive and the matriarch that is always by his side or a phone call away. Even when she leaves this life, we see his eventual-but-unexpected reunification with his beloved mother.

Conversations with Mother is cute. While it garnered a standing ovation from the much, if not all, of the audience, it felt to be geared towards an audience with grown children. I wasn’t able to connect to the characters, but I did thoroughly enjoy the evening watching the close-knit, sentimental relationship between mother and son. Despite how much Bobby’s mother disagreed with his choices, she maintained the supportive mother role. She knew when to put her foot down—and she was stubborn and controlling—but Bobby’s appreciation and need for his mother’s affection was just as evident when he was away at camp as a young child to when he was a grown adult with teenagers of his own.

Photo Credit: Carol Rosegg

Maria (Caroline Aaron) is an honest, straight forward, no-excuses and nothing-held-back mother. Her lines are comical and not forced in the way they could have been, which grounded both Maria and her relationship with Bobby. Aaron’s tone may have been flat, but her virtue and ability to move on from her own husband’s early death made Maria easily likable. Aaron and Doyle share a chemistry on stage that I am so glad was not lost. Again, another make it or break-it aspect of this production, since the story’s entirety depended on their shared relationship. And, on top of this, Doyle presents us with a believable, laughable, and endearing performance of decades of Bobby’s life.

Matriarch Maria and her son Bobby pass through decades of each other’s company—wanted or not. Maria shows up when he doesn’t want her to, and she makes Bobby figure himself and struggles out when he most wants her. It’s a story of growth, love, and acceptance. It’s seemingly an ideal relationship to mothers and sons that have a fractured relationship; it gives hope that when mother or son does something the other does not agree with, that they will still love and support each other, even with great distances.

While dates were projected onto a screen displaying backdrops and lighting, the years turning into passing decades seemed insignificant; I lost interest in what year it was. Years were coupled with a queue of “mom-lines” that set the theme for each scene of their relationship. I didn’t love these, but they were effective in driving Maria’s maternal assertions. Closets on-stage began being used as a place to change and prepare for big life events, transitions. This was more effective in guiding the audience through time while keeping them engaged–not losing them–as we watched Maria and Bobby enter new stages, together and apart.

“Tell me the truth and I won’t get mad” was the running line throughout the play, to the point where when Maria had reached her final year of life, she was the one asking Bobby to not get mad as she confessed to “killing” their family’s dog, decades before.

While Maria had five other children to dote on, it seemed as though Bobby was a sort of best friend to swoop in to help in time of financial and medical need, to boss around as the Italian Matriarch she was, and to show up to hold his hand as they watch the production of his first big play.

STARRING Matt Doyle (Bobby) and Caroline Aaron (Maria Collavechio).

Written by Matthew Lombardo. Directed by Noah Himmelstein.

Conversations with Mother is playing at Theater 555, 555 W. 42nd Street, New York, NY, for a strictly limited engagement until May 11, 2025. Runtime is approximately 85 minutes with no intermission. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Chain Theater’s Program 13 is part of its series of 24 Programs of one-act plays that support both new writers and actors of theater. Simple sets and a cacophony of stories over several weeks. Each group of one acts, some 4 a night, some 3, and some 5, depending on length, are presented on The Chain’s 36th Street stage.

It is giving, gracious, and formidable to present so many shows over several weeks. Scheduling and creating evenings with a huge collection of 94 new pieces alone is an achievement. And so, thank you to The Chain for this gift to so many playwrights, actors, and directors.

It also means that performances are not always balanced. Each evening can have one good piece, followed by confusion, followed by excellence, and so on. And that is the chance you take, as once again I must state that The Chain is open to engaging audiences in new pieces and writers. Bravo Chain.

Program 13 is an imbalance of stories and production value. The limitations were in the volume and clarity of the performers. Some of the performers were speaking below everyday volume, so the story they were trying to tell was lost. We, the audience, became so quiet, straining to make out what was being said, and unfortunately, we remained lost. Thus, the storyline was lost to us. When unable to create interesting, intriguing sets with the time limit and space, you must then rely on the performers and the words spoken to move the story forward more than ever. With nothing to hang onto, it leaves the audience in limbo.

The evening consisted of four one-act plays: Doors are a Hammers Best Friend by Jociel Tambone, FREE SEX! by Hassan Sharif, Hair Salon and Sam by Linda Herskovic, and One Night by A. Dean Bell. These shows all have merit in the stories and the characters, but the production left us hanging again and again. The laissez-faire of some of the performers left the words falling and not floating, definitely not connecting. Actors practically whispering meant stories could not be followed because we, the audience, could not hear them. The exceptions to the evening FREE SEX! by Hassan Sharif set in a prison, and “Hair Salon Sam” by Linda Herskovic, as you can imagine, set in a hair salon, are both stories of people desperate and trying to connect. The actors gave it their all, and so we, the audience, laughed and listened. “One Night” has as a very plausible and interesting take on getting so drunk that you are not sure if you committed a rape. The ending scene is powerful, and thus, I encourage the writer to go deeper with that. The two leads together wondering what happened, one a perpetrator and the other the victim, were enthralling. “Doors are a Hammers Best Friend” is a terrific concept – roommates stuck in their apartment because the front door won’t open – but this one in particular was hard to follow, and only at the end did we understand the relationship of the third person in the room, and by then it was too late.

I do want to point out the respect and importance of the role of the audience and staying for the entire evening to support not only the one act you particularly came to see but all of the pieces in the evening.

And I want to thank The Chain again for its commitment and support, its time and dedication, to writers, actors, and directors, giving them a chance to test their wings.

“Doors are a Hammers Best friend” by Jociel Tambone and Directed by Nicole Ulloa   With: Daisy Duarte, Kevin Guaman and Stiles Ramirez

“FREE SEX!!” by Hassan Sharif and Directed by France Jones  With: Carson Thomas, Daniel Baesler, Xavier Jefferson, Jameal Bailey, Mia Fritz, and Adelia Castillo

content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

In Jiggs Burgess’ Wounded, presented by SoHo Playhouse, the grief and rage of three people in a small, Texas town explode in a show that pulls no punches. Having won the 2024 SoHo Playhouse International Fringe Encore Theater Series Overall Excellence Award, Wounded comes to its Off Broadway run under the direction of Del Shores, acclaimed writer, director, and producer.

Katie (Kristen McCullough) is the beleaguered mother of Elizabeth, her thirteen year old daughter who was struck by a car at a young age and completely paralyzed. In one of their many outings to the park, Katie encounters Carrol (Craig Taggart), an older gay man with a luxurious fashion sense and a voice that’s a cross between Dolly Parton and Julia Child. He is also a nosy gossip who immediately annoys Katie. While she is guarded and high strung, Carrol projects a molasses-like ease, punctuated by high-pitched giggles at his own jokes. McCullough and Taggart deliver energized comedic performances with a particularly Southern, small town bent— throwing around “bless her heart”s and insults coated in politeness. They move between catty jibes and honest reflections on grief seamlessly, like a waltz between two compatible dancers. Taggart’s larger-than-life performance is magnificent, elevating every joke and bringing unexpected softness to sincere moments, and McCullough’s earnestness pulls at the heartstrings. Initially, I questioned the choice to represent Elizabeth, whom Katie affectionately calls “Sparrow,” as a doll in a wheelchair rather than having an actress. I wonder what the audience might have gained from being faced with the reality of a living, breathing person in this role who must remain on stage, in the same spotlight as her mother, and yet never be able to participate in a conversation that is largely about her. But this is not Elizabeth’s story. It’s Katie’s, and as much as she tries to treat her daughter as an autonomous person, it becomes clear that she also sees her as a broken thing to care for. Wounded doesn’t shy away from these morally gray areas, instead choosing to show how victims of tragedy can spread their misery and hurt to others.

We also see how empathy can sometimes be easier when we don’t know someone very well; when we don’t know the skeletons they keep in their closets. While Carrol comes across as a compassionate jester in the first act with Katie, we see a new side of him around Robert (Shaw Jones), a high school classmate and ex-con whom Carrol had an unrequited crush on. Jones looks the part of a former Texan homecoming king, and his immediate charm as Robert initially conceals the more sinister aspects of his character. If the first act was a waltz, the scenes between Carrol and Robert are a bull fight, with each man bringing out painful memories to taunt each other. As more about their shared past is revealed, the two morph from downtrodden friends to brokenhearted men with vengeful streaks. Wounded plays with the audience’s sympathies, never allowing us to rest easily in our conception of who was wronged and who inflicted the pain. Taggart and Jones are excellent scene partners, and they are mesmerizing to watch as they circle each other’s insecurities and lunge out at old wounds.

While some of the script felt like well-trodden territory, especially around homophobia in small towns, there were many beautifully crafted explorations of human connection and identity. In a particularly vulnerable moment, Robert shyly asks Carrol when he first knew that he was gay. Carroll responds with his signature, sharp laugh before explaining that he never had the coming out experience because he has always loved men. “Oh honey,” he says with a barbed slyness, “You might be gay. I’m a queer… And always have been.” At a time when we are seeing renewed attacks on queer people, and as stories like the kind told in Wounded are being suppressed, the show carries a poignant weight that is hard to shake even after leaving the theater.

WOUNDED – Written by Jiggs Burgess; Directed by Del Shores,

WITH: Kristen McCullough (Katie), Craig Taggart (Carrol), Shaw Jones (Robert)

Evan Frank (Set Design), Carter Ford (Light Design), Adam Matthew (Sound Design), Tori Moss (Production Stage Manager) and Miranda Shaffer (Assistant Stage Manager). Produced by SoHo Playhouse (Artistic Director Darren Lee Cole, Managing Director Britt Lafield) and Beard Collins Shores Productions (Emerson Collins, Louise H. Beard and Del Shores).

At SoHo Playhouse, 15 Vandam Street; (212) 691-1555, https://www.sohoplayhouse.com/. Through March 16. Running time: 2 hours 30 minutes.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Commissioned by Manhattan Theatre Club, Dakar 2000, by Rajiv Joseph, is a lie from beginning to end. The author lies to us for effect and the characters lie to each other and themselves, all leaving the audience on constantly shifting sand.

These lies we’re told are, “the guiding principle of most foreign policy.” Well thank you State Department, but this leaves the audience to hold everything at arm’s length, not sure what to trust, and not being involved nor care about the characters and their outcome. Without the personal charm of actor Abubakr Ali, this play would not be able to keep the audience’s attention.

The only honest thing on the stage was the set by Tim Mackabee which was built on a turntable and incorporated both indoor and outdoor settings. Its movement helped the story flow and added much-needed atmosphere to what could have been a stilted experience. All the dialogue takes place in confined spaces: an office, a rooftop, a bar, and a hotel room, and director May Adrales does a commendable job of creating movement (with the help of the set) within these confines.

It’s Y2K, on the eve of the year 2000, and many worldwide are standing by waiting for the world to end. US State Department employee Dina’s (Mia Barron) world has already come to an end with the bombing of the Tanzanian embassy in 1998 having lost several friends and the love of her life. She was supposed to be working at the embassy that day but was home with a hangover that saved her life. The investigation of the perpetrators has come to a standstill, “No longer a top priority,” and she is seeking revenge for the destruction of her world. Following the possible funder of the Tanzanian explosion, she is in Senegal. She feigns to get Peace Corps volunteer Boubs (Abubakr Ali) out of trouble for misappropriating government supplies to win his trust and in exchange for enlisting him in an espionage plot that involves, sedatives, disguises, breaking and entering, and fingerprinting an unconscious man to confirm identity.

These two characters never connect on any deep level but only feign to do so. The audience does the same.

—–

Dakar 2000, written by Rajiv Joseph and directed by May Adrales.

Starring Mia Barron and Abubakr Ali.

Technical: Tim Mackabee – Scenic Design; Emily Rebholz – Costume Design; Alan C. Edwards – Lighting Design; Bray Poor – Sound Design; Shawn Duan – Projection Design; Tommy Kurzman – Hair & Make-up Design.

Now playing at Manhattan Theatre Club, 131 W 55th Street, through March 23.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

The run time of the show is 90 minutes, with no intermission.

title.rendered: ON THE EVOLUTIONARY FUNCTION OF SHAME

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Talk about Food For Thought.  This is one of those plays to which people will refer in the future and say, “How come it took so long for this story line to appear?”

D. A. Mindell states in his program bio that “His work aims to contribute to a canon for transgender artists to explore the breadth and depth of opportunity that cis artists have been able to pursue for centuries.”

He has achieved that goal with this production and then some.

Adam, a transgender man, is pregnant.  This fact is introduced as a fait accompli.  There is no fuss, only fact.  Mindell does not spend time in exposition and expects us to keep up.  Adam (Cody Sloan) and his partner Fox (The understudy Marx appeared in this role on the day I saw this show.  He was superb.)  are visiting the office of Adam’s sister Eve (Kayli Carter) who is a scientist as well as a gynecologist.  Within the first few minutes of this scene we know that Adam adores both his partner and his twin sister.  The fact that he is pregnant is taken in stride – we are the ones who must catch up.

Mindell leads us down the path of first pregnancy jitters as they co-mingle with family disturbances and medical research.  Everything matters, and problems are revealed with laser precision.  Eve’s research partner Margot (Imani Russell) is pulled into the mix as an autistic voice who cuts through the detritus Mindell reveals.  Everybody has an opinion, and no one holds back.

We learn that Eve and Margot have been focusing on genetic research (the name of the company is the Eden Project) that could change the lives of many an unborn as well as offer a myriad of tests that Adam might choose to have.

Adam does not choose.  You should pardon the expressions, but Adam is adamant.  See what I did there…?

As more information on Eve’s research is revealed, the thread of the beaded garment holding everyone and everything together begins to fall apart.  Mindell and director Jess McLeod team up to present us with a tale of enormous consequence told in straightforward language.  These characters are at once loving and sloppy, tender and clumsy, reassuring and suspicious.  This is elegant ensemble work that honors the author’s intention.

The tale of the contemporary Adam and Eve is bookended by the tale of the original couple.  Jordan Barbour as Adam 1 and Elizabeth Ramos as Eve 1 acquit themselves well as our ancestors.  The question for me is why were these characters included?  They add little or nothing to the contemporary story.  I am certain I am missing something here, but honestly, the contemporary play has more than enough food for thought.  Yeah, yeah I know “Shame” is in the title, but these two stories did not connect.

This contemporary tale is a smorgasbord of ideas that will accompany you for a long, long time.  It stands on its own with no apologies.

Get over to Second Stage Theatre and leave your pre-conceived notions at home.

ON THE EVOLUTIONARY FUNCTION OF SHAME

by D.A. Mindell, Directed by Jess McLeod,

Jordan Barbour, Kayli Carter, Elizabeth Ramos, Imani Russell, Cody Sloan and Ryan Jamaal Swain and on the day I saw this production Marx appeared as Fox.

Scenic Design by You-Shin Chen, Costume Design by Hahnji Jang 장한지, Lighting Design by Barbara Samuels and Keith Parham, Sound Design by Bailey Trierweiler

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.
